The proposed upgrade to the LHC and its associated experiments will enable the study of rare processes with enhanced precision. A key focus for these experiments will be on exploring rare kaon decays, with the potential to detect a small, previously undetected charge imbalance in $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays. To facilitate this research, a brief examination is conducted to assess the current understanding of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay modes, specifically charge misidentification in $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays and the resulting impact on the measurement of $CP$ violation in the $B^0_s$ sector. A quantitative analysis of charge fluctuations leads to an estimated overall error of 1.5%, while charge misidentification accounts for an additional 0.5% error due to limited multiple scattering data. A further investigation into $B^0_s\rightarrow \phi\phi$ decay modes is also presented, with possible $CP$ violation phases in $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ and $B^0_s\rightarrow \phi\phi$ decay modes assessed in separate measurements to minimize the influence of charge fluctuations on $CP$ violation determinations. A preliminary estimate of the required integrated luminosity for these measurements yields 13 $ {\rm fb}^{-1}$ for $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays and 60 $ {\rm fb}^{-1}$ for $B^0_s\rightarrow \phi\phi$ decays, with an expected error of 3.5 degrees in the $CP$ violation phase $|\cos \delta _{ CP }|$ in $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays and 5.9 degrees in $B^0_s\rightarrow \phi \phi $ decays. A strategy is proposed to enhance the precision of these measurements further. A proposed technique for determining the $B^0_s$ flavor at production is investigated to reduce the impact of initial state $CP$ violation on these measurements, with a resulting error reduction of 10% in the $CP$ violation phase $|\cos \delta _{ CP }|$. A related issue with charge fluctuations in the kaon decay mode requirements for same-flavor $B^0_S$ production suppression techniques is also examined, with possible techniques for reducing this effect discussed. The main focus is on examining the existence of solutions to a discrete version of this system, as well as on establishing that these discrete solutions converge to the solutions of the original system. These findings are highly consistent across various energy ranges and cannot be accounted for by standard models of cosmic-ray distribution and propagation. Our discovery demonstrates the unique capabilities of ground-based cosmic-ray detectors in studying the statistics of extremely energetic particles on a large scale and the unique insights they can gain into the distribution and composition of high-energy sources. This study introduces a novel time-varying model called Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregression with external covariates, which seamlessly combines two models: a time-varying Poisson autoregressive model and a switching model. This innovation allows for flexible temporal changes in parameter values, as well as in the model's own specification, making it an extremely useful tool for capturing complex temporal dynamics in count-based time series data. We have successfully tested this new model on artificial data and real-world datasets, and have found it to significantly outperform the current state-of-the-art time-varying Poisson autoregressive model in terms of model selection criteria. Furthermore, this model has been applied to the analysis of football match outcomes, where it revealed intriguing temporal variations in the underlying parameters, in addition to revealing the importance of external covariates, such as weather conditions, and the dynamics of team performances. One step further, we have also derived an expectation-maximization algorithm for estimating the model's parameters from the data. One of the paper's sections is dedicated to methodological extensions of the TVPAR model, where we have explored the application of the model to over-dispered count data, as well as discussed possible modifications of the model, including the addition of lagged dependent variable effects and non-Gaussian external covariates. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that combines the benefits of neural networks and descriptor fields to enable efficient and robust object manipulation tasks. NDFs incorporate a unique orientation-agnostic and translation-invariant representation, incorporating both local and global features that characterize objects throughout manipulation tasks. This representation allows for accurate object matching, even when orientation changes, and demonstrates significant improvements in performance over conventional methods including PointNet and RelationNet. We further show that NDFs' intrinsic property of ignoring irrelevant global features enables faster learning for tasks that value local feature extraction, such as classification. We demonstrate the versatility of NDFs by successfully applying them to challenging object manipulation tasks on two popular platforms, DeepMind Lab and simulation environments created with Mujoco and PyRobot. Our results show that NDFs' orientation-agnostic representation and efficient learning capabilities are crucial for achieving low failure rates in manipulation tasks. We open-source NDFs to facilitate further research and development in object representation and manipulation.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct tasks: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We integrated the two processes, leveraging correspondence learning to guide projection grouping and used a proposed compact intermediate cue representation to reduce computation. Experimental results showed that our apparatus outperformed the competitors across five datasets. Notably, a marked performance boost was observed across three datasets when evaluating on the more challenging real-world scenario. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyangyin/DeepHMap++.pdf.

Our research extends the concept of eigenvector centrality to multi-layered networks by taking into account the reliable calculation of node significances across different layers. In multi-layered networks, information can flow between layers, allowing for the spread of influence across different networks. However, this flow also creates opportunities for the dissemination of misleading information. To address this challenge, we developed a method to identify the most prominent nodes that could serve as trusted sources of information, by analyzing the centrality of nodes across different layers. This approach enables us to determine the significance of nodes within each layer and calculate their overall significance, taking into account the reliability of information transfer between layers. We found that our method can distinguish between the distribution of central nodes and the distribution of node significances, as well as detect the layers that contribute to the calculation of overall node significance. Furthermore, we found that the reliable calculation of node significances across different layers is crucial for accurately determining the component structure of multi-layered networks, and that our approach can be compared to existing methods through simulated network models. We also explored real-world applications of our method to multi-layered networks, including electoral districts and scientific collaboration networks. Our research provides a foundation for further investigation into the dynamics of multi-layered networks, as well as ways to improve our method and generalize it to other complex systems. Our code is available online at https://github.com/AmirHajizadehDarbin/eigenvector_multilayer.

This study investigates how spheres interact with running water by being flushed with water at various speeds. It was observed that at higher speeds, water penetrates the spheres in a consistent and predictable manner. By analyzing these patterns, the study identifies three distinct regimes of water penetration. In the middle speed regime, a steady state of water infiltration is observed, where the water forms a curved interface with the sphere and moves at a constant rate. To better understand this intermediate regime, also known as the levesque regime, mathematic models were developed to describe the curved interface and calculate its rate of change. Two such models were tested and found to be accurate in predicting the rate of change of the curved interface. One model accounts for the forces of friction and pressure exerted by the water, while the other model includes the effect of water's surface tension. Although the models are complex, they can be simplified to reveal the fundamental factors that influence the rate of change of the curved interface. The study finds that the rate of change of the interface is directly proportional to the square of the water's speed and its surface tension, and is inversely proportional to the friction exerted on the sphere. Additionally, the models demonstrate that the rate of change of the interface is independent of the sphere's size. The models were further tested to validate these findings and they were found to be accurate. The study also analyzes the conditions under which the water's speed becomes so high that it causes the sphere to break and release its contents. The models developed in this study can be compared to existing research on the subject, which includes the works of Levesque, Quinberry, and Torrey. We investigate the possibility of a Type IIB string theory effective field theory containing a generic $\theta$-term, given that it has a complex free energy. We determine the conditions under which a $\theta$-term is viable within the framework of an effective field theory. The results indicate that the complex free energy condition must be met for a $\theta$-term in an effective field theory involving a cubic interaction. However, the condition can be met for a $\theta$-term in a effective field theory involving a quadratic interaction, which occurs in the presence of a certain symmetry being broken. The specific case of a Weyl rescaling symmetry being broken is explored, and it results in the appearance of a $\theta$-term involving the Gravitino coupling. The outcome is also viewed from the perspective of an effective field theory involving a $\theta$-term, which yields the presence of a massless fermion in the spectrum. Despite their advantages, generating these states poses a significant challenge, particularly when utilizing Gaussian quantum processes. In this research, we demonstrate that single-photon facilitated coherent states can be created through the interaction of a beam splitter, a coherent light source, and a quantum system known as a bosonic integrator, which is capable of converting Gaussian states into non-Gaussian forms. By adjusting parameters, we can prepare states that facilitate the detection of a single photon, effectively converting the coherent light into a single-photon facilitated coherent state. Furthermore, this setup allows for the generation of these states in both continuous and periodic forms. This finding offers insights into the behavior of non-Gaussian processes and provides a means for generating specific non-Gaussian states, a crucial step in evaluating the functionality of quantum systems that detect single photons. This research also highlights the potential of beam splitter-based systems in generating state-specific conditions, a capability that can be expanded to other non-Gaussian states, thereby contributing to the development of measurement tools with high precision. We introduce a technique for creating polynomial models using linear regression as a foundation.  This approach, which we refer to as PRP for short, takes a linear regression model and generates a Taylor series expansion to create a basic polynomial model.  Additionally, this model can be augmented with terms identified by an integer programming-based technique, which targets local fit improvements by analyzing residuals.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to individual data sets, where it consistently outperforms the linear regression model based on various evaluation metrics.  We also examine this approach on a real-world hyperelastic material prediction problem, where it yields results that compare favorably to a commercially available solution.  We provide access to the code used in this study at https://github.com/ghp EfficientPolys.

Reddit's vast community allows for diverse discussions to take place within subgroups, based on users' personal connections, occupations, or geographic locations. Prior studies classify users into the Big Four Groups: political, occupational, interest-based, and geographic. Our research examines the significance of categorizing users by geographic location within Reddit, often overlooked in misinformation studies. We propose the term "Big Geographic Sort" to describe this classification. The study determines the Big Geographic Sort's implications for misinformation spread by identifying correlations between user group classifications, analyzing posts on Reddit forums, and conducting an experiment to simulate misinformation distribution. The results reveal that users sorted by geographic location tend to share information with other users with similar local preferences, thus increasing the likelihood of misinformation being shared within close-knit communities. Furthermore, the study finds that users from larger cities are more susceptible to spreading misinformation than their counterparts in smaller cities. The findings suggest that targeting ads to influence users in geographic areas where a piece of information is widely accepted can actually accelerate the dissemination of that information within those areas. The study also highlights the significance of user group classifications based on personal connections and occupational groups in limiting the spread of misinformation. The research utilizes an original Reddit dataset consisting of 10 million comments across 200,000 articles and incorporates theoretical explanations from information systems theory, network theory, and psychology. The study also highlights the Big Geographic Sort's broader applications in understanding user group classifications, including in offline settings. The study discovers four key factors that influence the degree of misinformation's spread: user group classifications, popularity, credibility, and geographic diversity. A complex field theory is defined as a set of classical Euler-Arnold equations parametrized by a Lie algebra, potentially extended by higher-order differential equations derived from the conformal spinfulness principle. This framework is used to demonstrate the occurrence of intrinsical difficulties within two-dimensional conformal field theories, specifically the Chern-Simons gauge theory. A direct connection is established between the fundamental algebra and the conformal field theory's intrinsical challenges, demonstrating a comprehensive set of Euler-Arnold equations that a conformal field theory must satisfy by definition. Furthermore, this framework enables the identification of intrinsic challenges within topological conformal field theories, offering insights into the subtle distinction between topological conformal field theories and other conformal field theories. A simple example, a U(1) gauge theory based on a Riemann surface with a toroidal boundary, is presented to illustrate the complexity of such theories in complex spaces. This involves a nonlinear equation that, when simplified to a linearization, loses its intricate nature and simplifies to a hyperbolic Laplace-Beltrami equation. This equation, although coherent, is not an Euler-Arnold equation and therefore does not qualify as a complex field theory. This particular case is unique and does not generalize, whereas the general case of a U(1) gauge theory is equivalent to the Abelian Chern-Simons theory on a compact spacetime. This leads to an important identification of an integral invariant that these types of theories possess in compact spacetimes. This invariance is linked to the topological nature of the underlying Riemann surface and can be determined through a topological quantization condition. This condition is based on the compactness of the spacetime and involves the topological charges of the boundary components, as well as a novel type of topological charge associated with a complex boundary component known as a branch point. This can be thought of as a singular point in the complex spacetime where the topology breaks down rather than being destroyed, and it possesses a unique set of characteristics that distinguish it from usual singular points and points at infinity. This case of a U(1) gauge theory based on a Riemann surface with a toroidal boundary also provides an opportunity to explore the interconnection between the complex spacetime, the conformal field theory, and the physical properties of the theory. This is achieved by implementing a Wick rotation that converts the complex spacetime into a Euclidean spacetime and examining the relationship between the Euclidean spacetime and the conformal field theory

We outline the components that make up an MTS, highlighting the key elements of a automated testing framework that includes test cases, a test driver, and a system under test. We also explore the various methods available for testing conversational agents, discussing both automated techniques and those that involve human participation. Although research exists on evaluating chatbots, such studies are often limited to subjective analyses by human evaluators. In contrast, an MTS enables the objective evaluation of conversational agents through automated means. We review the existing literature on MTSs, noting that researchers often refer to them as testbeds or chatbot evaluation platforms. One prominent example of an MTS is the Microsoft Conversational Test Bed, a comprehensive platform for designing and executing tests across various platforms, including desktop computers and virtual reality devices. We also examine the standards and best practices for evaluating conversational agents, outlining the key criteria for assessing chatbots at an individual level as well as at an institutional level. Furthermore, we explore the various contexts in which conversational agents are used, identifying potential safety-critical domains like transportation and healthcare. The integration of electric vehicles is becoming increasingly common and significant. This report examines the impact of privately owned electric cars on a power grid's resilience. We developed a decision-making framework that employs multi-agent optimization techniques to determine the most effective strategies to maintain the grid's stability and reliability in the face of disturbances. Our analysis utilized the IEEE 24-bus test system and showed that incorporating electric vehicles into the grid can lead to energy loss reductions and significant improvements in resilience. However, we found that a grid's stability is not always improved when electric cars are present and that a dynamic change in driving patterns can either help or hinder the grid's performance. Our research highlighted potential issues with the current design of the grid and suggested that a more complex transportation network should be considered in modeling the impact of electric vehicles. Ultimately, our work provided a foundation for further research into the optimal placement of electric vehicles, switching techniques, and the performance of distribution networks, particularly in areas with cold climates. This study included a technical appendix detailing the derivation of key mathematical formulas used in our analysis. This report is targeted towards a technical audience with expertise in mathematics, optimization, power systems, and transportation engineering. Coxeter groups comprise a broad category of mathematical groups that extend beyond the symmetric group framework, utilizing a variety of generators and associated intersection operators. The fundamental theorem of Coxeter groups in category B, as observed by Bolibol, attributes even permutation groups to the product of mirror reflection groups. This study expands on Bolibol's finding by classifying the odd permutation groups within the finite Coxeter group of type B. Specifically, it demonstrates that the group of odd permutations can be expressed as the product of reflection groups in a different arrangement, namely the alternating group, coupled with the hyperoctahedral group generated by raising 2 to a power equivalent to the number of input variables. This new formulation enables a direct link to the fundamental theorem of Gilbert and Reingold. Furthermore, this study also examines the generalization of the foundation theorem for the Coxeter group of type B, incorporating a detailed analysis of its components including the M\"obius function, the foundation poset, and the associated polynomial. The resulting expression can be viewed as a specific case of the general principle, which is validated by examining the characteristic polynomial of the adjacency matrix. The expansion of the fundamental theorem in the context of the Coxeter group of type B is also demonstrated through a concrete example, namely the hyperoctahedral group of order 486. Additionally, this study proves that the ring formed by the Coxeter group of type B under the operation of polynomial multiplication is Euclidean. Reconstructing cosmological parameters relying on the cosmological evolution of Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) rely on mapping their distribution through light cones. The distribution of SNe Ia is influenced by gravitational lensing, causing multiple images of a single cosmic event that can vary in brightness by several magnitudes due to the effects of mass distributions between the observer and the events. We calculated the distribution of SNe Ia magnitudes distorted by lensing in a light cone, considering a model consisting of a perfect sphere with uniform mass distribution. We found that the standard lensing formula overestimates the effect of lensing, and a new formula that takes into account the effects of the curve of the light cone is necessary. We applied this correction to the Pantheon SN Ia data set and found that the distortion in magnitudes is minimal, amounting to a difference of up to 0.2 magnitudes. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that this effect is recoverable through Bayesian analysis, and the recovered value for the Hubble constant is 69.6 km/s/Mpc with an error of 1.4, while the matter density $\Omega_m$ is 0.279 with an error of 0.019, and the neutrino density $\Omega_\nu$ is 0.0013 with an error of 0.0004. Finally, we conclude that the influence of lensing distortion can be recovered from SN Ia data, and future larger data sets will yield even more precise results. The approach we used to analyze the Pantheon data set can serve as a model for analyzing larger data sets consisting of multiple supernovae surveys combining SN Ia data with other cosmic distance indicators. The code used in this analysis can be made available upon request. The recovery of lensing distortion from SN Ia data also opens the door to analyzing the mass distributions of large groups of galaxies and the distribution of mass and light across the sky, and may have applications in the study of gravitational waves, the behavior of matter at the edge of bound systems, and the composition of dark energy. The way we calculated the recovery of lensing distortion also allows for the analysis of data sets consisting of SN Ia data with the addition of other cosmic distance indicators, such as giant elliptical galaxies, and opens the door to the study of the distribution of mass and light across the sky, and the composition of dark energy, as demonstrated in the appendix. The code used in this analysis can be made available upon request.

The recent rise in kidney transplants coming from incompatible donors has highlighted the need for advancing matching strategies. Initially, selection criteria focused solely on matching blood type and immunological compatibility, but now, techniques like desensitization treatments and expanded criteria for donor kidneys are being utilized. This study aims to analyze and compare the outcomes of transplants originating from compatible and incompatible sources, with a focus on patients whose donors possess a blood type antigen HLA-A2 or HLA-B7. A retrospective examination was conducted among 128 patients at our institution who underwent a kidney transplant between 2006 and 2011. The results revealed that patients who received kidneys from incompatible donors experienced a higher mortality rate within the first year post-transplant and had a lower kidney function over the ten-year study period. Furthermore, survivors with HLA-A2 mismatch experienced a higher risk of rejection and lower ten-year graft survival compared to those with a match. In contrast, HLA-B7 mismatches did not appear to affect graft survival or function. In conclusion, our data highlight the importance of distinguishing between different HLA mismatches, as only some may be considered equivalent to compatible transplants in terms of outcome. This finding is pertinent for developing guidelines for prioritizing kidney transplants and has implications for patients with HLA-A2 compatibility who may benefit from a B non typing protocol. The rise in incompatible transplants has the potential to address the growing demand for kidney transplants, but it also generates new challenges, including the increased risk of rejection, and highlights the need for improved matching strategies, desensitization techniques, and better outcomes for grafts obtained from incompatible sources. In the context of current practice, it is essential to redefine what is considered an acceptable risk of rejection, as this may vary based on individual preferences and values, and it has significant implications for how quality of life is assessed in clinical trials. Ultimately, more research is necessary to address these issues, with a focus on developing better outcomes for incompatible transplants, expanding the available kidney pool, and enhancing our understanding of what constitutes an ideal acceptance of incompatible kidneys. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word representations learned through the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Dictionary, a widely used resource for capturing the emotional content of words. We establish a mathematical framework to study the embedding of dictionary words, revealing their representation structures and categorizing the embeddings of positive and negative words based on their semantic meanings. Furthermore, we find that many word representations fail to adhere to their intended linguistic definition, as numerous synonyms of the same part of speech possess disparate embeddings, often with a negative correlation between their negative and cosine distances. Additionally, we discover representations that exhibit a linear relationship, often in a non-monotonic pattern, between the frequency and cosine similarity of word occurrences. Moreover, the paper demonstrates that many of these patterns hold constant even as word representations are updated using additional data. We also analyze the embeddings of a subset of words that convey opposing polarities, discovering that their representations often occupy mirrored locations in the semantic space. We propose a straightforward approach to address the issue of disparate embeddings of opposing polarity words by simply swapping the negative embeddings. Our results show that this method enhances the consistency of these words' embeddings and increases the frequency of correct polarity predictions made by a neural network. Our study highlights the shortcomings of current word representation learning models, suggesting they do not adequately capture the intended linguistic definition of the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Dictionary. We propose a new approach called Adversarial Hypernymy Reduction (AHR) that develops a model specifically tailored to accurately classify the polarities of hypernyms. Our results indicate that AHR outperforms standard approaches when evaluated on a range of tasks including sentiment analysis, hypernymy prediction, and semantic similarity evaluation. Our research is supplemented by a publicly available repository containing the mathematical framework, reference code, and guidelines for replicating our results. We also discuss possible avenues for future research presented in the paper. Our findings highlight the difficulties encountered when applying pre-trained language models without consideration of their linguistic assumptions, demonstrating the value of rigorously examining the underlying mathematical properties of these models. In multiagent competitions, we seek a rationalizable equilibrium that is resistant to attacks or deceitful play. However, identifying a strategy profile that is both an equilibrium and collectively rational for all players is challenging, as it requires analyzing each player's private thought process. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce an efficient algorithm that determines whether a specified strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium in polynomial time, following a natural line of computation mirroring the decision process of players. In contrast, for combinatorial auctions, we observe that a related approach yields a more complex analysis involving a more intricate examination of each player's individual thought process. An epidemic spread can lead a network to deteriorate, potentially causing it to repel future epidemics by transforming into a more robust state through the reduction of vulnerable elements. To investigate the paradoxical effect of disease-induced deterioration, we apply a paradigm from physics known as the "weak localisation paradox" to epidemiological models. By using discrete, autonomous nodes that spread disease and deteriorate independently, we created a model that reflects this paradox. Simulating this model reveals a peculiar phenomenon: the spread of disease eventually leads to a state of maximum resilience, where the speed of disease transmission slows down before eventually dying out. However, this outcome depends on the timing and intensity of deterioration, with different patterns emerging based on the random arrangement of nodes and their individual response to epidemics. To capture these complex patterns, we applied random matrix theory to simulate an infinite, dense network of nodes. In doing so, we found that the network's resilience could switch between different levels of susceptibility to epidemics, a phenomenon we believe has implications for other complex systems influenced by local interactions and random arrangements. Nevertheless, the underlying principles can also be represented by simple mathematical equations that describe the delicate balance between the spread of disease and a network's self-improvement, thereby ensuring a state of maximum resilience. Ultimately, this model can be applied to a wide range of phenomena, from the distribution of resources in spatial environments to the spread of misinformation on social media. Theoretical representations of these models can be valuable tools for achieving a deeper understanding of these complex systems and can potentially lead to novel interventions that manage and improve the performance and resilience of these systems. The simulation data for the discrete network model and the associated matrices are available for download at https://datadrive.uni.lu/EpsteinGroup/Epidemics-on-Restructuring-Networks. To improve policy enhancement using replay data, a proposed method in this study assigns different weights to past data frames based on their age and distance from the current policy, then uses these weights in a variance-reduced experience replay buffer to calculate the policy gradient. Unlike existing approaches that treat all past data equally, this method treats data frames closely matching the current policy with greater importance, thus reducing the impact of outdated information. In addition, the proposed algorithm eliminates the need to maintain an exploration-exploitation balance by continuously encouraging policy improvement, without compromising too much on performance. Experimentation with the proposed method on various tasks demonstrates improved policy enhancement using value-function based methods, and the possibility of achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art baselines using better-rated simple models. The proposed algorithm is particularly effective for difficult tasks like difficult levels of Atari games. The code for the proposed algorithm is available at https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/policy-enhancement.

The LHC is poised to explore the substructure of jets, both through the study of subjets and minor systems, which could signal new physics beyond the Standard Model. This article discusses the theoretical expectations for minor systems, including baryon and meson production, and reviews current and future LHC experiments' capabilities to detect these systems, with a focus on the search for supersymmetry. As the amount of collision data increases, smaller systems like charm mesons embedded in jets are also an important area of study, and experiments are optimizing protocols for their detection. A comprehensive discussion of minor systems, including both general searches and targeted studies of supersymmetry, is presented, with an analysis of current searches using data from the Tevatron and LHC, and an examination of future detection possibilities using the HL-LHC and future colliders. This article also reviews techniques for object selection, production mechanisms, and signal and background estimation, with an emphasis on charm mesons embedded in jets. Although primarily focused on supersymmetry, this article also discusses other physics beyond the Standard Model that can be investigated using minor systems, and provides an overview of ongoing and future experimental and theoretical work in this area. This article is intended for both experienced physicists and graduate students, with an introductory focus on theoretical and experimental basics. As such, it is hoped that this article will serve as a comprehensive reference on minor systems at the LHC. This article is based on the proceedings from the 21st Cracow Epiphany Conference, held in January 2020.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre reveal sources that have remained inactive for an extended period, and the notion that these sources are situated in binaries containing a neutron star is intriguing. If a neutron star binary has a long recurrence time for outbursts, it is considered "quiescent". To determine if these binaries contain neutron stars, we need to establish their recurrence periods accurately. Although significant research exists on the subject, there is room for improvement, particularly in analyzing the Luminosity Function for outburst recurrence periods. In this paper, we re-examine the outburst data of these binary systems using a comprehensive approach and concentrate on determining the recurrence periods for outbursts, outburst luminosities, and the distribution of luminosities to understand the characteristics of these binaries and distinguish between them and those that contain a neutron star. By comparing various distribution models, we found that the outburst luminosity distribution follows a power law with a specific index, and the recurrence period for outbursts can be predicted using the luminosity function, which displays a specific overall pattern in the range of luminosities relevant to these sources. Furthermore, we investigate the possibility of outburst recurrence periods being influenced by the binary star system's mass rather than luminosity, and analyze the possible characteristics of these sources, including those that may remain inactive, by matching the observed data to theoretical models, and discuss the implications of these findings for the environment within the Galactic Centre. Lastly, we discuss the possible explanations for the absence of low-mass binary systems within the Galactic Centre and the implications of these findings for the theory of neutron star binary mergers and the surrounding environment of the Galactic Centre.

THz spins and phonons share analogous characteristics with electrons and the oscillations of the lunar tides, and their interactions are crucial in quasiparticle dynamics. The framework of time-dependent perturbation theory is used to investigate the interaction between a discrete vibration (spin vibration or electron-phonon interaction) and a broader background of phonons and spins, resulting in the coupling of a single pulse to the system, combined with a continuous field representing the background noise. This interaction takes the form of a Lorentzian function, where the width is determined by the frequency and intensity of the background noise. When the intensity of the background noise is increased, the width of the Lorentzian function also increases, causing the decay of the interaction or the width of the resulting sidebands. This result is analogous to the decay of a lunar tide signal caused by the presence of chaos in the lunar orbit. This finding suggests that the intensity of the background noise, which is comprised of the inherent dynamics of the system, determines the magnitude of the interaction between a discrete vibration and the surrounding environment. This result has implications for the interpretation of experimental data involving the interaction between a particular vibration and the surrounding noise, and highlights the importance of considering the intrinsic dynamics of a system when analyzing its interaction with the external environment. This approach can also be applied to the study of the interaction between a particular quasiparticle and the surrounding sea of particles, or the interaction between a particular mode of vibration and the background noise of the system. This result can be applied to a wide range of systems, including magnetic materials, superconductors, and biological systems, and provides a starting point for the development of new theoretical models of interaction dynamics. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on predicting two overlapping faces from a single image, with each predicted face representing a different head orientation. We demonstrate that modeling face orientations in this self-altering framework offers numerous benefits, including the facility to handle large head orientations and the capability to create synthetic data with different head poses. We have developed a novel neural network called SADRNet to perform two-facing predictions, featuring a U-shape connection that facilitates the exchange of information between the two faces and a dropout-based sampling mechanism in its pipeline. We have also introduced the self-altering 3D face reconstruction task at the workshop and the conference venues, along with SADRNet as the submitted methods. Our research has been conducted using a large dataset of reconstructed 3D faces, combining three individual datasets with a unified framework, and we have made this combined dataset available to the public. We have evaluated our approach on multiple datasets, revealing substantial gains in metrics related to precision, the description of head poses, and the quality of reconstructed faces. We have made SADRNet's source code and the face-reconstruction-at-head-poses-task dataset available online.

Compression of perturbations requires a second generation of inflation, which can arise when the scalar field reaches the top of a hill within the potential. However, as this scenario results in PBH formation, it's inevitable that the subsequent phase will give rise to overexpansion of perturbations. On the other hand, compression of perturbations can also develop during an phase known as oscillatory inflation, which is triggered by a field displacement. Compression of perturbations can then lead to PBH formation, while overexpansion hinders this process. Ultimately, our research reveals the necessity for multiple discrete displacement values to accomplish PBH formation through inflationary perturbation compression, and highlights the significance of further cosmological perturbation analysis in an oscillatory inflationary phase following a hill in the inflationary potential. In this work, we aim to gain insight into the underlying mechanisms of Hamiltonian Neural Networks by examining whether it is possible to approximate the gradients of a loss function using these networks. Our investigation begins by providing a historical context of HNNs and related developments. We then outline our approach, which involves utilizing HNNs to estimate the gradients of a stochastic logistic regression loss function. We calculate the estimated gradients by taking the derivatives of the loss function's inputs with respect to its inputs, using the connections and activations specified in the HNN model. We then utilize these estimated gradients in the same way as traditional stochastic gradient descent algorithms. Our study reveals that networks similar to HNNs can successfully estimate the required gradients, thus enabling the updating of the model's parameters. We also discover that adding residual connections to HNNs greatly improves the accuracy of these estimates. Furthermore, we observe that these networks can be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, and that reinforcement learning can be employed to overcome this challenge. We demonstrate the generality of our findings by successfully estimating the gradients of a complex policy network in the context of the CartPole game. Our research also highlights the relationship between HNNs and the reparameterization technique used in stochastic gradient descent algorithms, as well as the possibility of constructing Hamiltonian networks from scratch that mirror the dynamics of continuous latent variables used in algorithms such as Hamiltonian Neural Networks, Bayesian neural networks, and meta-algorithms, without relying on the reparameterization technique. We conclude by suggesting that HNNs can be viewed as an extension of Hamiltonian dynamics systems that incorporate the gradients of a loss function, and propose the term "Hamiltonian Gradient Systems" to describe this concept. We anticipate that this proposed framework, which we term Hamiltonian Gradient Systems, may have far-reaching implications for enhancing the efficiency of gradient estimation methods, as well as for the development of new learning algorithms in the realm of machine learning. We also explore this concept in the context of two specific games, and demonstrate the benefits of using Hamiltonian Gradient Systems in these instances. We anticipate that our findings may serve as a foundation for future research on the subject of Hamiltonian Gradient Systems. We make our code available online at https://github.com/ghrasoul/HNN.

The fabric space |M| associated with a given piecewise linear manifold M has been a well-defined concept in differential topology for a piece of research by the 1970s, thanks to the work of a single mathematician, Raoul Bott. This space represents the collection of all possible triangulations M can take, treated as points in a topological space, and it's particularly useful for identifying equivalent triangulations and capturing the intrinsic properties of M. However, as the concept gained less popularity over time, its development stalled, and only a narrow band of the theoretical framework remains clear to us today. In contrast, a more comprehensive theory of a fabric space can be constructed using a different mathematical framework, known as stratified topology or simplicial topology, that provides a broader understanding of this concept. This new perspective also leads to an important variation of the fabric space, labeled the monodromy group $\Gamma(M)$, that can be used to define equivalence relationships between the triangulations of M, resulting in the classification of M as a union of its triangulating components. Furthermore, this novel perspective on the fabric space enables us to determine if a specific triangulation is valid or not, simply by examining its connection to an existing reference triangulation, and it provides a straightforward method for generating all possible adjacent triangulations given an existing one. In addition, this general framework can be applied to study the nearby triangulations of any simplicial complex, making it a significantly expanded version of its original counterpart. In total, this extended theory of the fabric space, along with its associated monodromy group, offers a powerful tool that can be used in a wide range of areas, from geometry and topology to physics and biology, where the analysis of complex structures and manifolds is continually performed.

This research investigates the capabilities of future high-energy electron-positron colliders equipped with luminosity of 10 ab^-1 to discover double Higgs boson production with subsequent decays to b-quarks and tau-leptons, a process extremely sensitive to beyond-Standard Model Higgs interactions. Utilizing Effective Field Theory, we evaluate the cross-section for this process and identify its components sensitive to Higgs couplings. For a 100 GeV center-of-mass energy, we find that double Higgs production in the b tau_tau channel is feasible with approximately 5.6 ab^-1 of data at an average luminosity of 3.5·10^33 cm^-2 s^-1, primarily limited by ggH subprocesss. This involves reinforcing the Standard Model prediction, particularly in mis-identifying tau leptons, and presenting production cross-sections for reference, which compare to the predicted 0.693 pb in the Standard Model. Additionally, we determine the minimal number of double Higgs events required to discover new physics interactions, which ranges from approximately 200 to 5000, varying depending on the interaction modified. Understanding the relationship between the external shape of organs such as the liver and their internal structures is crucial for medical applications. In particular, analyzing the attachment of liver surfaces to its internal vessels and tissue volumes can help in identifying pathological areas. However, accurately determining this relationship is complicated by the soft, fragile nature of the liver. Previously proposed methods to determine liver surfaces from limited internal data relied on time-consuming iterative computational techniques or required the assumption that the surface normal of the external shape is parallel to the direction of internal data vectors. In this paper, a novel algorithm is presented that uses a pre-trained machine learning model to determine the relationship between the external and internal data of organs, specifically the liver. This model enables the efficient computation of liver surfaces from limited internal data, even in cases where the available data is insufficient to determine the surface uniquely. Experimental results using real MRI scans demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of computational speed and accuracy in determining liver surfaces. Furthermore, the proposed framework allows for better alignment of the surface with abdominal wall boundaries, enabling safe removal of artificial edges that bound the vascular structures and tissue volumes within the liver. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for multiple computer vision tasks, including action recognition and volume reconstruction. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through light-field, stereo, or monocular images remains challenging due to the complexity and partial nature of real-world data. In response to this difficulty, researchers have explored the use of intrinsic metrics to estimate scene flow, relying on the intrinsic properties of the animated three-dimensional environment. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to metric learning that enables the automatic development of customized intrinsic metrics in relation to the motion trajectories, without requiring neighbor data. This approach leads to a self-guided scene flow estimation framework, without the need for additional training data. The proposed framework utilizes sparse noise during training to create a robust model, resulting in the estimation of a high-quality baseline scene flow, as demonstrated through extensive experiments on real-world datasets. Compared to conventional methods, our proposed framework in combination with a specifically designed network, surpasses existing state-of-the-art performance on datasets involving light-field and stereo images. Moreover, our proposed framework in combination with a commonly used network, achieves comparable performance to conventional methods while monitoring the accuracy of action recognition, as demonstrated through experiments on monocular image datasets. The proposed framework, alongside its code and models, is available for public access. The development of realistic and comprehensive evaluation datasets is essential for further advancing the field. The proposed framework serves as a starting point for future research, as indicated by the numerous possible enhancements, including the use of multi-scale motion trajectory data and the integration of scene flow with action recognition networks. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We demonstrate the efficacy of this model in multiple benchmark scenarios by comparing it to established methods, showing that it offers significant improvements in both accuracy and low-energy performance. Moreover, the model's simplicity enables easy integration into existing spike-based hardware platforms, facilitating seamless deployment in real-world applications. We also provide a comprehensive overview of RNNs, discussing their background, fundamental principles, and variations of the model, in addition to delving into the specifics of Spiking Random Neural Networks. Lastly, we address potential challenges and future research directions for this model, including enhancements to its sampling mechanism, validation of its performance across various hardware platforms, and investigations into its ability to handle difficult, dynamic time-series analysis scenarios. We hope this revised and expanded version of our paper will appeal to a broader range of readers, sparking further innovation and discovery. We then establish a one-to-one correspondence between ideals in a specific commutative semiring and the subgraphs of a particular type of strong, locally regular graph, namely one derived from a set of Hamiltonian circuits in a cubic graph. This equivalence enables us to translate mathematical problems related to this strong, locally regular graph into combinatorial problems associated with the associated semiring, thereby gaining insight into its ideal structure. This construction encompasses not only Hamiltonian circuits in a cubic graph but also other graph structures as well. Seismic waveform inversion aims to create high-quality images of the Earth's internal structure by analyzing seismic data from experiments. However, achieving accurate results faces significant challenges due to the complexity and partial randomness of the Earth's composition. To address this issue, researchers have proposed modifying the target waveform by inverting synthetic data, making the problem more feasible, but also more difficult to solve, as it requires a more precise model. In this study, researchers demonstrate that a common waveform inversion challenge can be overcome and that a simplified model is sufficient for certain seismic data. Furthermore, by utilizing finite difference methods to simulate seismic data, researchers are able to introduce random variations into their model and demonstrate that standard waveform inversion techniques can handle these models. This research also explores two approaches to modify the target waveform: one that corrects the model by inverting the difference between actual and simulated seismic data, and another that amplifies the waveform that results from finite difference simulations. To solve this problem, the research utilizes a complex algorithm that breaks down the time-domain waveform into multiple frequency bands and applies an inversion technique to each band separately. This approach allows for the introduction of random variations into the model and provides better results than standard techniques. To further validate this complex algorithm, the research compares it to a simpler and more traditional approach, known as waveform waveform inversion, and finds that it provides more accurate results in most cases. This study also explores issues related to data quality and the effectiveness of different algorithm parameters, and concludes by discussing potential applications and related research. This scheme utilizes a reflective surface to facilitate efficient data and power transmission between pairs (P1, P2,...) by optimizing both communication channels and the surface's reflecting coefficients. Our study examines coexistence problems in this integrated network, focusing on channel interference and the surface's optimal design. To enhance performance, two optimization approaches are explored: one using game theory to minimize interference and another utilizing artificial bee colony optimization to maximize the integrated information and energy gain within a specific area. Our results show that both optimization methods lead to improved performance compared to a conventional D2D system. Furthermore, this integrated network finds additional applications in areas such as intelligent transportation, where it can be used for safety message dissemination. Our research also discovers that a certain level of surface precision is necessary to achieve maximum performance gains. Our study paves the way for integrated information and energy D2D transmission in various scenarios, offering multiple potential use cases. In experiments involving particle collisions, neutral long-lived particles could escape detection if they interact too weakly with standard matter. A combination of missing energy and specific decay patterns might indicate the presence of these particles, offering a way to discover them even if they escape detection. To effectively find these particles, it's crucial to understand how likely it is that they'll be detected in various scenarios. This study evaluated the effectiveness of the Belle II experiment at detecting particles that might escape detection due to their weak interaction with matter, specifically neutral long-lived particles produced in processes involving beauty mesons. To calculate this detection rate, it used theoretical models that assume these particles interact with standard matter through a new force called a "axion-like interaction". The results are presented as minimum visible cross-sections, which indicate the level of particle collisions required for a detection in a specific experiment. It's been shown that with an average luminosity of 10 ab^-1, the Belle II experiment can efficiently detect particles that interact weakly with matter, specifically neutral long-lived photons produced in processes involving beauty mesons, with a minimum visible cross-section of 100 nb. Our analysis of contextualized language models, using case studies from Wikipedia articles, reveals that they may misinterpret shifts in word meanings due to contextual dependence. We found contextualized models often confuse local variations in word senses within the same text as evidence of semantic change, neglecting the importance of external context. Furthermore, we observed they tend to overestimate the complexity of word meanings, interpreting multiple possible senses within the same text as distinct senses. These issues become particularly pronounced when using methods that rely on intrinsically recognizing context, such as contextualized clustering. To accurately detect semantic change, we recommend experimenting with different models and incorporating structural knowledge from external sources, such as syntactic trees, to better capture the structure of word meanings and context. This experience serves as a cautionary tale for researchers studying the dynamics of language, reminding them that context is a multifaceted element with far-reaching implications. The theory of superradiance suggests that rotating black holes or compact objects should emit intense electromagnetic radiation due to interaction with external electromagnetic fields. This effect is likely to occur in the far environment of massive quasars and their associated black holes. We examine the relationship between ultralight bosons and quasar spins using the concept of superradiance, and investigate the possibility of a non-monetary signature of a universal ultralight boson population. If such a population exists, we anticipate the ratio of Lyman-alpha to H-alpha emission lines to exhibit a clear pattern of variation with wavelength, driven by the interplay of line broadening and the characteristic wavelengths of these emission lines. This prediction can be tested using a an emerging database of quasar spectra based on data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Galaxy Evolution Explorer. If ultralight bosons are inferred to be present, we estimate that their mass must lie within a narrow range, perhaps between $4.5\cdot 10^{-13}$ and $4.5\cdot 10^{-12}$ eV, and we anticipate the ratio of Lyman-alpha to H-alpha emission lines to exhibit a periodic oscillation with a specific length scale that is determined by the spin of the associated black holes. This expected behavior can be confirmed or refuted via a single observation of a quasar spectrum via a spectrograph with a suitable wavelength resolution. If confirmed, this discovery would provide evidence for a widespread distribution of ultralight bosons and clarify the underlying mechanics of superradiance. Moreover, this finding would enable us to calculate the mass of these bosons based on their fundamental properties, as well as to verify the assumption that they are ubiquitous. This approach can be applied to a vast array of ultralight scalar fields that are thought to be present in the far environment of the universe, including its cosmic neutrino background, its quantum fluctuations, and its various condensates, as well as to a vast array of collective modes that could be present in hadron or atom condensates, and to a vast array of hypothetical particles that could be present in the far environment of the universe, including axions, monopoles, and photons. This novel method of investigating the characteristics of ultralight bosons via quasar spins offers a non-monetary signature that is distinct from the gravitational waves generated during their cosmological production and subsequent evolution, and provides a more sensitive and accurate means of detecting these bosons, as well as collecting comprehensive information about their properties

A distinctive and widespread neural development pattern called interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) is observed in the embryonic brain. Consisting of alternating upward and downward movement along radial glial fibers, this pattern provides the source material for the formation of distinct neural types and contributes to the expansion of the brain. While the underlying causes of a variety of patterning events in the developing brain have been successfully modeled using mathematical approaches, the specific case of IKNM remains particularly resistant to analysis. In the current study, we use a non-invasive high-resolution imaging technique to provide a comprehensive examination of IKNM in the developing retina of zebrafish. Through a careful analysis of nuclear movement at the individual level, as well as at the level of brain development, we revealed that the direction and speed of nuclear movement are randomly distributed, contradicting the long-held belief that it follows a directed and rhythmic pattern. As a result, we can model this pattern using a simple diffusion algorithm, which also enables us to evaluate the random movement of nuclei at different stages of development. Our findings demonstrate that the degree of nuclear movement disorder is greater at more advanced stages of development and that a change in this movement pattern is necessary for brain development to proceed in an proper and stable way. Notably, our research shows that a pure rheological brain model, which links the movement of nuclei to the formation of the brain, can result in a developed brain that is stable, smooth, and free of defects. However, once we introduce a component that allows for the formation of neural types, the model indicates that a specific level of disorder in the movement of nuclei is required for type formation and brain stability, a finding that is consistent with observational data. Additionally, our data reveal that retinal development is linked to the movement of nuclei and the associated cell division, and that the termination of this movement is necessary for the retina to develop properly. Moreover, our research demonstrates that a diffusion model of the movement of nuclei is necessary to accurately predict areas of tissue expansion and type formation, and that this model can be used to evaluate and predict the outcome of abnormal movement patterns on the development of the brain. Our current study provides a mathematical approach for analyzing a complex development pattern in the brain, and as such, it has significant implications for understanding a variety of patterning events in the developing brain. The findings of this research have been applied to the retina of zebrafish, but they can be used to model brain development in other organisms as well. We develop a new stochastic differential equation that represents the behavior of polar fluids under stress in dimensions $d$ greater than $2$, with particular emphasis on the impact of certain obstacles and the spatial characteristics of these obstacles. Our primary goal in introducing this equation is to demonstrate that it has a steady-state representation, which can be determined through a specific transformation that reflects the distribution of the obstacles. This representation takes the form of a stochastic differential equation with a frozen disordered structure, where the stress behaves as a continuous parameter that affects the equation, even though the disorder is actually deterministic. Our main mathematical achievement is to prove that this stress equation has a unique solution that is bounded for all positive dimensions $d$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the parameters of the polar fluid's static properties converge to a set limit as time approaches infinity, which can be determined by examining the characteristics of this fluid's disorders. Our results also hold true for a related model called the conical one-dimensional stochastic flow, which has been previously studied by the authors in a prior paper. The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to adapt identity verification methods to an online environment.  As a result, countries like Indonesia need an efficient way to convert their national ID cards from a physical format to a digital form.  Convincing Indonesians to embrace this transition will depend heavily on making the process of scanning their ID cards straightforward and hassle-free.  To accomplish this, an application was developed which uses Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology to extract information from Indonesian ID cards, with a natural language processing-based editor to correct any errors made during the scanning process.  This application provides a user-friendly interface that guides users through the scanning and editing process and allows the saved data to be downloaded in a compatible CSV format for easy integration into various systems.  The developed application was put into use and proved not only to be compatible with different operating system types but also to efficiently convert Indonesian ID cards to a digital format.  The data obtained from this process was used to create a dataset that can be utilized for further research and development of Indonesian ID card OCR technology.  The dataset in question consists of 5000 manually corrected strings, 2000 scanned Indonesian ID cards, and 10 different font types used on these cards.  This research was conducted with the support of the Indonesian Government, specifically the Directorate General of Applied Technologies, Ministry of Research, Technology, and Higher Education.  This research was also presented at the International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Pattern Recognition, and Robotics held in Langkawi, Malaysia, from the 8th to the 10th of November, 2022.  The developed application and research findings have significant implications for the transition to a National Digital Identity in Indonesia. This paper focuses on the time-dependent, driven quantum harmonic oscillator to demonstrate the application of path integral techniques within Markov Chain Monte Carlo frameworks. Furthermore, we derive explicit, numerical values for the time-dependent, driven quantum harmonic oscillator within both constant and cyclic driving scenarios. Our temperature-and-fluctuation-corrected method enables highly precise calculations of average energy across a wide range of temperature values. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP impact, researchers were able to determine the rotation velocities of these asteroids and found them to be rising due to the YORP effect as predicted by theory. In particular, the rotation velocity of Geographos is notable for increasing most rapidly, which can be attributed to its dark surface reducing the YORP slowdown mechanism's effectiveness, and also making it a promising candidate for rotating rapidly enough to break apart. While the YORP effect is a critical force shaping the rotational dynamics of small asteroids, it's essential to note that it's not universal and can be opposed by other forces such as gravity, tides, and volatilization, as seen in the case of Geographos. To better understand the YORP effect's impact, researchers recommend continuous light curve monitoring and astrometric observation of these asteroids to analyze their orbits and variable rotation states. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying these computable functions to solve specific problems involving infinite strings, including determining computable functions that can distinguish between infinite strings, the structure of which changes over time, and the identification of infinite strings with a specified property. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases often relies on a small number of high-rate transmission events between an individual and a large group of people. This common phenomenon, known as a "super-spreader event," can significantly contribute to the rapid spread and persistence of epidemics. In the context of an epidemic, we define a super-spreader event as a situation where a single individual transmits the disease to three or more people within a short period of time. This definition is supported by mathematical modeling, which shows that the rate at which a single individual transmits the disease to others plays a more critical role in leading to an epidemic than the overall rate at which the disease is transmitted from one person to another. We have developed a mathematical model that incorporates super-spreader events and found that epidemics are more likely to occur and spread more quickly when super-spreader events happen frequently. We have also found that the likelihood of an epidemic increasing in severity is higher when the rate of high-rate transmission events is greater, although this trend reverses in certain situations. Additionally, our analysis indicates that increasing public health measures can lead to a decrease in the rate of high-rate transmission events, which in turn can cause the epidemic to spread more slowly. Our model has been validated through comparison with historical data from a cruise ship outbreak, and our results have implications for various other contexts, including the management of epidemics, the control of population growth, and the understanding of the transmission dynamics of diseases. Moreover, our model provides a framework for analyzing the effects of different strategies for managing super-spreader events, which can occur in a wide range of situations and are often driven by the behavior of individual individuals. Our analysis also highlights the difficulty of predicting the occurrence of super-spreader events, which can have a significant impact on the spread of an epidemic, and the importance of taking these events into account when modeling the transmission dynamics of diseases. Our model has been applied to analyze the outbreak of a specific epidemic, which was characterized by a high number of high-rate transmission events, and our results show that the model can accurately represent the complex transmission dynamics of this epidemic, which was influenced by various factors, including the spatial distribution of the individuals and the time-varying patterns of super-spreader events. Our analysis of this epidemic has also provided valuable insights into the key factors that led to its spread and persistence, and our results can be used to guide the development of effective strategies for managing similar epidemics in the future. Our research has implications for various other contexts, including the management of epidemics

The potential presence of bias in vector magnetic field maps, especially in areas with weak field strengths, is a significant challenge. This issue may lead to incorrect conclusions about the behavior of magnetic fields in areas around sunspots, where field strength changes most significantly. We investigated the presence of bias in both the magnitude and direction of vector magnetic field maps, using synthetic data, a model solver, and observations from the Solar Optical Observatory. Our findings suggest that the $p$-mode resonance noise in the Stokes $V$ spectra affects the bias in the field direction, especially in areas with weak field strengths, although the impact on the field magnitude is minimal. We also discovered that the noise in the azimuthal angle has a larger effect than expected and that a larger beta value is necessary to reduce this impact. Our research utilized the RESIDUAL technique to remove noise from the spectra, which resulted in a significant reduction in beta values, indicating that noise reduction can significantly alleviate beta-related biases, especially in areas around sunspots. Furthermore, we found that the bias in the field direction remains minimal, while the effect on the field magnitude becomes more pronounced in these areas. Our analysis suggested a larger beta value of 3.5, whichcorresponds to a sensitivity to the specific noise filter used, rather than a particular beta value. Our study utilized a simple model to demonstrate that the beta-related biases primarily affect the range of field directions, rather than the field strength distribution. Finally, our research highlighted the importance of considering the range of field directions when analyzing the distribution of field strengths, which may have implications for similar problems in solar and stellar astrophysics. Our code is available upon request.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, focusing on tasks with partially shared input structures.
A novel approach, unsupervised retrieval-based augmentation, is proposed to achieve this by utilizing unlabeled samples from the target dataset to acquire new knowledge.
This method involves pairing models with relevant existing examples to expand their knowledge base, which is achieved through a contrastive learning objective in the latent space of the model.
Through experimental validation on multiple datasets and scenarios, our proposed method is consistently shown to demonstrate significant improvements in various evaluation metrics. The code for this work is publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/Unsup-Cross-Task.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, especially in Hubei province. In this environment, online rumors about COVID-19 exploded in China, threatening the country's epidemic control and causing confusion among the public. To address this issue, the Chinese government launched a special campaign to combat the spread of online rumors in February 2020. Our research focuses on exploring the mechanisms behind the spread of online rumors and assessing their impact during the COVID-19 outbreak in China. To achieve this, we collected and analyzed data on 4,531 COVID-19-related rumors reported by China's network of 30,000 citizen journalists. Our findings reveal that the primary mechanism behind the spread of online rumors in China involves manipulating user engagement through deceptive content, coupled with inadequate detection and filtering technologies. Our impact assessment reveals that approximately 22% of all rumors spread quickly, 13% caused confusion among the public, and around 25% had a significant impact on epidemiological control policies. Our statistical analysis indicates that the speed of rumor spread is influenced by factors such as news authenticity, the size of the online audience, and the extent to which authorities enforce epidemic control measures. In contrast, the extent to which rumors confuse the public or affect epidemiological control policies is primarily driven by biases among fact-checkers rather than other factors. Our research highlights the significance of combating fake news and the importance of maintaining the transparency of dissemination algorithms in order to prevent the spread of online rumors in China during the COVID-19 outbreak. In addition, our findings emphasize the need for fact-checkers to be impartial in order to effectively control the impact of online rumors. Our approach provides a framework for analyzing the impact of COVID-19-related rumors and offers policy advice to the Chinese government on how to control the spread of online rumors in China during the COVID-19 outbreak. In conclusion, our research findings can be applied to similar situations in China or elsewhere in the world where the spread of online rumors during the COVID-19 outbreak poses a significant threat to public health and epidemiological control measures. From a theoretical perspective, our research provides new insights into information diffusion dynamics, reinforces our understanding of the mechanisms behind the spread of online rumors, and offers a framework for assessing their impact on public health and epidemiological control policies. Our research also offers practical recommendations on how to develop effective dissemination algorithms and maintain the transparency of fact-checking biases in order to control the spread of online rumors in China during the COVID-19 outbreak.
