A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining planetary nebulae with similar luminosity properties. This method's effectiveness in reducing reliance on nebulae with extremely high luminosities is particularly beneficial, as it minimizes the impact of systematic errors associated with this luminosity range. Furthermore, as planetary nebulae spectra often contain abundant iron and magnesium lines with well-known standards, this approach avoids the previous limitations of relying solely on nebulae with extremely high luminosities by utilizing a more comprehensive sample, including lower luminosity planets. This more inclusive sample reduces the influence of individual stars and galaxies that could introduce random and systematic errors into the measurements. The application of this method to the Fornax3D data set, which comprises 839 planetary nebulae linked to 34 galaxies in the Fornax cluster, has yielded a mean distance modulus of 10.96 ± 0.08 (statistic) ± 0.05 (systematic) for the Fornax cluster, which is consistent with previous measurements obtained using other planetary nebulae standards and globular cluster populations. The minimal required assumptions for this method, coupled with the vast amount of detailed astrophysical information available from analyzing planetary nebulae, make this approach a valuable tool for deriving precise distance measurements to galaxies. The comprehensive data set of planetary nebulae found in the Fornax3D survey, along with the relevant measurement equations, is available online. The accuracy of this approach has been further validated by comparing the planetary nebulae based distance measurement with the tangent point distance obtained from the Hubble Space Telescope for three galaxies observed using the Fornax3D survey. The recovery of the well-characterized iron abundance from the planetary nebulae spectra also enables the estimation of the metal content of the gas linked to the galaxies, the abundance of which has been found to be nearly indistinguishable from the abundance of the galaxy stars. The inspection of the planetary nebulae linked to specific galaxies has revealed a distinctive population of nebulae linked exclusively to one galaxy, the elliptical galaxy FCC 309, which may be examined in the context of a vast planetary nebula population linking multiple galaxies. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of sensitive patient data through various medical applications, producing data streams that need to be analyzed in real-time. These streams, once processed, must be securely stored in compliance with medical regulations. We have developed a prototype data processing engine, called LifeStream, tailored to the specific needs of medical practitioners. This engine processes both real-time and recorded data and is designed with efficiency and interoperability in mind, allowing seamless integration with popular operating systems and medical applications. Furthermore, LifeStream complies with the standards set by medical establishments, ensuring secure and reliable data storage. We have tested LifeStream on actual data streams captured from a hospital and found it to be highly effective, supporting large-scale real-time analysis and securely managing massive amounts of stored data. We believe this engine provides a valuable solution for hospitals seeking to establish efficient and secure real-time data analysis capabilities. The underlying technology of LifeStream has been made publicly available on GitHub, ready for customization according to individual needs. The results of our testing are also presented in detail, demonstrating LifeStream's performance on various evaluation metrics. The potential applications of LifeStream extend beyond medical environments to any setting that involves real-time analysis of time-sensitive data streams. The name of the project, LifeStream, is a combination of the words life and stream, reflecting its purpose as a life-saving data stream processing engine. The source code of LifeStream has been developed using C++ and MySQL, offering a high-level interface for real-time data analysis and a low-level interface for managing database operations. The performance of LifeStream has been compared to that of Apache Flink, a renowned open-source data processing engine, showcasing LifeStream's superior performance in various workload scenarios. The results of our evaluation highlight LifeStream's capabilities as a real-time data analysis engine, capable of processing large amounts of data across multiple clusters while ensuring reliability and reducing storage requirements. The potential improvements of LifeStream are discussed, focusing on its ability to handle bursty data streams, its storage management system, and its scalability in multi-cluster environments. The future development of LifeStream is proposed, including the development of a graphical user interface, the integration of machine learning algorithms, and the enhancement of its storage management system. The results of our evaluation are presented in the form of graphs, providing a visual representation of LifeStream's performance across different workload scenarios. The performance of LifeStream is compared to that of Apache Flink on multiple evaluation metrics, offering a comprehensive comparison of the two data processing engines. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional space. Specifically, we determine the equations that these curves must satisfy in a semi-Euclidean $R^4$ space and provide an alternative representation of these curves using the Frenet frame. Furthermore, we examine the (1,3)-Bertrand curve and its associated curve, establishing that they both lie on the same surface defined by its mean curvature. Lastly, we establish that this surface is synclastic if the space is Euclidean, whereas it becomes complex or umbilical in the hyperbolic or light-like space respectively. Additionally, we determine the specific (1,3)-Bertrand curves in these spaces and provide numerical examples for the hyperbolic space. Lastly, we discuss the differentiation of the (1,3)-Bertrand curve and its associated curve, as well as the relationship between the curvature and torsion of these curves. Moreover, we establish that these curves can be distinguished based on their differential properties and the values of their curvature and torsion. Lastly, we provide an approach to analyze the (1,3)-Bertrand curve and its associated curve in an arbitrary semi-Riemannian space.

Re-training a neural network with a new loss function is thought to require re-initializing the neural network, due to the significant impact of the early layers being sensitive to the input data. This conviction has been a cornerstone of machine learning theory since the early days of neural networks. However, this research challenges that notion by demonstrating that the early layers of a pre-trained neural network are actually more resistant to changes in the loss function than the late layers, which are more influenced by the presence of a dropout layer. Moreover, we discovered that the performance of a neural network can be improved by modifying the loss function during training, with the optimal time of this modification correlated to the level of dropout utilized. When the dropout level is 0.5 or higher, our experiments showed that simply using a squared loss function leads to a comparable or better classification performance compared to using a cross-entropy loss function. We believe that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of neural networks and provide a way to tailor loss function modifications, which could also lead to a reduction in the required size of neural networks. Our findings are supported by a specific analysis of a neural network trained with a squared loss function, which demonstrates that this type of loss function leads to the early layers acting as feature learners and the late layers acting as classification learners. We also discovered that transferring the early layers from a neural network trained with a squared loss function can lead to performance gains, which is a more efficient method of transferring those layers from a network trained with a large dataset. Our research was conducted using a neural network trained for classification, but we believe that our findings are applicable to other neural network architectures and purposes. The simulation shows that the formation of crystalline lamellae is more effective when the material is stretched to a higher degree, resulting in the orientation of these lamellae. However, if the material is subjected to larger deformations, the formation of lamellae becomes less efficient as they break apart, and the material experiences significant thinning. The simulation also reveals that the surface tension between the crystalline and non-crystalline regions plays a crucial role in the formation of the microstructure known as the "fishbone" arrangement. When the simulation focuses on the larger scale of the material sample, the simulation demonstrates how surface tension affects the material's overall thickness and the efficiency of the crystallization process. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. The importance of incorporating spin-polarization of the superconducting order parameter is further demonstrated by investigating the influence of finite momentum pairing, showing that this type of pairing always leads to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility or results in a first-order phase transition, depending on the topology of the Fermi surface. The implications of this analysis for other materials exhibiting finite momentum pairing and displaying a diverse range of magnetic susceptibility responses are also discussed. The presence of external strain on the material is found to delay a topological transition to higher doping levels, while external pressure exerts an opposing influence, potentially converting a nematic to a chiral phase in the presence of electron-electron interaction. The theoretical framework developed in this analysis is further applied to finite length scales, with the formation of a suboxide layer influencing the magnetic susceptibility response in the bulk material. The possible occurrence of finite momentum pairing in the related material Bi$_2$Se$_{3.12}$ is highlighted, with this type of pairing capable of resisting decay into a uniform state even in the presence of random point defects or dislocations. The possible experimental observation of this state of matter is also discussed, with results showing that the most suitable method for detecting finite momentum pairing would involve an analysis of the response of the material to applied stress, in conjunction with an investigation of the superconducting order parameter using scanning tunneling microscopy. Traditional coherent CPM detection requires a reference symbol, which can be inconvenient to implement, especially in scenarios with limited bandwidth. This research explores methods to enhance the differential delay of conventional non-coherent differential CPM detection. Initially, we review the fundamental limitations of this detection method, which can result in a differential delay of up to half the symbol period, potentially causing significant interference in various applications. To address this issue, we consider two main scenarios: one with an odd number of pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) samples and an even number of PAM samples. For the latter case, which presents an ongoing research challenge, we propose a novel detection technique based on the application of the difference operator to the PAM samples, combined with a signal shaping technique to further improve performance. In the case of an odd number of PAM samples, we examine and optimize an existing detection method known as differential delay CPM detection. Our proposed technique's performance is evaluated through simulation, demonstrating its efficacy in various CPM formats. Our research finds that the proposed technique can achieve a differential delay of up to 7 PAM samples in 4-PAM CPM, and an even number of PAM samples in 2-PAM CPM, among other formats. Our results also indicate that our proposed technique can be adapted to support negative differential delays, which can be particularly useful in certain applications. Our research offers a novel detection method that can be directly employed by various systems, such as radio frequency fingerprinting, where the system configuration allows for an odd number of PAM samples. To investigate this contrast, we analyze a stochastic general relativity model in a compact, symmetric spacetime setting using a quantum cosmology framework. By applying a quantum cosmology technique, we define a quantum capability metric that gauges a spacetime's capacity to develop a stochastic, self-sustaining cycle. Ultimately, we establish a relationship between this capability and a spacetime's average scalar curvature, thereby providing a concrete example of a stochastic general relativity equation that can be applied to research compressed spacetime scenarios. Additionally, we determine a critical compressibility threshold for a specific geometric spacetime configuration, offering insights into the compressibility of spacetime at both microscopic and macroscopic levels. Furthermore, we find that this capability metric can be linked to a matter-filled spacetime scenario, thereby extending the research to include scenarios beyond pure vacuum compressibility. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common knowledge reasoning rules comprised of five distinct elements: cause-and-effect relationships, intentions behind actions, physical characteristics, emotional influences, and intent behind statements. This comprehensive dataset addresses various reasoning challenges, such as identifying intended recipients of messages, understanding the purpose behind performing physical tasks, and determining the physical consequences of those actions, among others. At the core of ATOMIC lies a versatile framework consisting of five separate databases, each tailored to address a specific reasoning challenge. We assemblage these databases into a unified whole to present a comprehensive atlas of everyday common knowledge reasoning rules, demonstrating the existence of explicit rules governing typical situations and providing a foundation for evaluating and operating on common knowledge. Our experimental evaluation reveals that incorporating elements from ATOMIC leads to significant improvements in the accuracy of reasoning tasks performed by machine learning models, particularly in tasks related to intention and inferences behind actions and statements. We make ATOMIC available to the public for further exploration and utilization. Our code and the dataset are accessible at https://github.com/yashkanoola/Atomic.

One of the most compelling applications of quantum computing lies in its ability to accelerate linear algebraic problems through iterative linear solvers, particularly the use of the Quantum Linear Algebra Package (QLAP). QLAP includes operations for resolving linear systems, matrix vector multiplications, and the transformation of matrices. However, the lack of a reliable and efficient classical-to-quantum conversion process for these tasks poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose the NISQ-HHL program, which incorporates a range of portfolio management strategies to optimize the performance of the Hamiltonian Simulation component of HHL. We test and evaluate NISQ-HHL on four distinct case studies, including applications in Quantum Natural Language Processing and Quantum Machine Learning. The results show that this program delivers a genuine performance improvement of 10-50% on real-world devices, and we anticipate these achievements will serve as a foundation for further advancements in QLAP. The code for NISQ-HHL is available online at https://github.com/luowenber/NISQHHL. The QLAP framework and accompanying examples can be found at https://github.com/luowenber/QLAP. The code for the case studies can be accessed at https://github.com/luowenber/CaseStudies. The performance metrics for real-world devices are based on actual simulations with the IBM Quantum Experience System, and the graphical illustrations were created using the Cirq, Qiskit, and TensorNetwork toolkits. To enhance speech recognition using deep learning, it's beneficial to incorporate transcriptions in the training process, especially when working with large amounts of audio-visual data. This approach leads to advances in multiple areas including error reduction, resource extraction, and task extension. However, implementing this method raises challenges, primarily due to the asynchronous nature of speech and text, which complicates modeling techniques. To address this issue, a new multi-modal training method called Speech-Text Aided Learning (STAL) is proposed, incorporating a bidirectional focus mechanism to synchronize speech and text processing. This focus mechanism, utilizing forward and backward attention networks, allows for efficient exchange of features between speech and text. Additionally, STAL includes a Leaky Residual Connection (LRC) to remedy the performance degradation observed in the initial stage of training. Experimentation with the proposed technique on two separate speech recognition datasets demonstrates significant accuracy improvements. Specifically, it achieves 8.15% relative improvement in correct phrase recognition and 12.68% in word error rate (WER) compared to conventional techniques. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits robust performance under limited visual data, showcasing its versatility in real-world applications. The proposed STAL framework can be employed in various speech recognition scenarios, providing a versatile and accurate solution. The code for this project is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ChengxiangTan/Speech-Text-Aided-Learning.

This article uses combinatorial and analytic methods to analyze the set of natural numbers represented by the sum of their digits in base $k$, added to a shift of $k$. We are interested in the structure of this set for a given $k$, and how it changes as $k$ increases from 2 to infinity. Our analysis focuses on the number of elements in the set, its smallest element, the largest element, and the elements' asymptotic behavior in the context of $k$. We establish lower and upper bounds for the number of elements, showing they are roughly square roots of $k$ for large $k$. We also determine the shift value that maximizes the number of elements and identify the asymptotic behavior of the smallest and largest elements relative to $k$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the set is asymptotically congruent to the set of natural numbers represented by the sum of their digits in base $k$, for large $k$. Our results extend and improve earlier findings of Diaconu and Iorga and of Iorga. Our approach to achieving these results involves using parking space configurations and a combinatorial formula derived from them. We also discuss the connection between this problem and the concept of Ehrhart polynomials. Additionally, we provide an alternative, simpler proof of the asymptotic behavior of the number of elements in the set. Moreover, we analyze the same set but with a shift of $k^2$, which enables us to determine the asymptotic behavior of the number of elements in the set and show that it is less than the square root of $k$ for large $k$. Our results include an estimate of an upper bound for the number of elements in the set and demonstrate that the set is asymptotically congruent to the set of natural numbers represented by the sum of their digits in base $k$, added to $k\sqrt{k}$. We also find the shift value that minimizes the number of elements in the set and provide an estimate of an lower bound for the number of elements in the set, which is also based on its smallest element. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold below which conductivity is inhibited due to the accumulation of charge or phase slips. The charge inhibition phenomenon is thought to result from the presence of residual defects within the nanowires, especially at low temperatures. This study involves precise control of conductivity and phase slips in NbN nanowires through applied gate voltage in a 2DEG-based structure. By examining conductor-like Kondo effects and taking into account the influence of the gate-controlled environment, our results show that the threshold behavior can be shifted by an order of magnitude, far exceeding explanations based on coherent quantum phase slips or Coulomb obstruction. Instead, our findings suggest that the conductor-like Kondo effect plays a key role in charging the nanowires and thus influences their threshold behavior. Additionally, our research involves initializing the nanowires in a superposition of a qubit, allowing for the precise control of their threshold behavior through the Shottky field generated by the qubit. This breakthrough enables the reliable production of coherent phase slips through the application of a gate-controlled voltage, providing a solution for generating entangled pairs of Josephson circuits in the coherent state. This achievement expands our understanding of the conductor-like Kondo effect and related phenomena, while also opening the door to complex quantum simulations and the creation of large-scale, distributed, and controllable many-body systems. This study involves experiments and theoretical modeling of the conductor-like Kondo effect and related phenomena in superconducting nanowires, with supporting analysis conducted using precise numerical simulations of the S-N-S nanowire structure. This work can serve as a foundation for future research on the conductor-like Kondo effect, including theories such as the coherent quantum phase slips and Coulomb obstruction, as well as related phenomena like the conductor-like Kondo effect in the charge space, the atomistic theory of this phenomenon, and the possibility of initializing the nanowires in a superposition of a qubit. This study involves a combination of experimental measurements and theoretical analysis, with the underlying physics explained in detailed appendices. This research was conducted by various co-authors, with the lead author making significant contributions to the project, including developing the initial idea, guiding the experimental approach, analyzing the data, and overseeing the theoretical modeling and simulations. In applications such as video surveillance and remote operations, view video forecasting can be very useful by predicting the view of a situation or an object from a different camera angle than is currently being observed. In this paper, we outline the rules and constraints of an innovative forecasting task called Innovative View Video Forecasting (IVVF), which involves predicting a future video from a specific camera angle that is different from the current perspective. We then present a novel approach based on dual representation, which uses both spatial and temporal transformation to forecast future videos from both the current and a different camera angle. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in IVVF and IVVF-NOise on datasets Davis and IVVF-Noise, surpassing the performance of current state-of-the-art methods DFN and AT2DKN. Our evaluation also shows that our method's ability to forecast innovative views as noise reduces the gap with IVVF-NOise. Our code is available online at https://github.com/lingyu2016/IVVF.

In this research, inter-orbital interaction was demonstrated using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), which allows for the precise examination of spatial electron interactions in solids. To accomplish this, a 2D solid with evenly spaced orbital patterns was created under high pressure and low temperature, allowing for accurate alignment of orbitals and inter-orbital distance control. As a result of combining STM and angular resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPEPS), the spatial arrangement of electron clouds, local energy levels, and inter-orbital interaction could be visualized and measured in real time. Specifically, the transition energy between orbitals at a particular site was directly measured as approximately 0.4 eV, which is in close agreement with theoretical predictions of around 0.3-0.5 eV. Furthermore, the results show that inter-orbital interaction can be influenced by external means, such as light and electric fields, which allows for precise control of solid state orbitals and their interaction. Airborne transmission of diseases in confined spaces is a significant concern, and the level of mixing assumed in existing models can greatly impact predictions of infection spread. To address this issue, we propose a novel airborne transmission model specifically applicable to closed environments, which takes into consideration the distinct patterns of airflow and the limited mixing effect. We have particularly adapted this model to simulate the movement of aerosol transport and mixing on an urban bus, and have conducted in-depth mathematical and numerical analyses of the model. Our study reveals that the model exhibits oscillatory behavior, and by constructing a suitable Lyapunov function, we prove that the model's equilibrium state is asymptotically stable when respiratory rate exceeds the rate of air exchange. Furthermore, we derive an explicit condition for this stability in the specific case of urban bus transmission. Additionally, we provide a theoretical estimate for the time it takes for the system to reach its steady state, as well as numerical data obtained through laboratory experiments on urban bus transmission. Our findings also compare the accuracy of models with full mixing to the proposed model, both numerically and based on laboratory data, and have found that the proposed model is significantly more accurate in predicting the dissemination of a pathogen on an urban bus. This is particularly true when the bus is moving at a fast pace, due to the creation of airflow turbulence that hinders the mixing of aerosol transport. We introduce a novel regularization technique that leverages the concept of Lipschitz continuity to improve neural networks. In order to apply optimization methods on neural networks, we suggest a straightforward yet effective approach called Lipschitz Consistency, which can be incorporated into the learning process using backpropagation. We demonstrate that enforcing Lipschitz consistency along with maximizing classification accuracy leads to improved performance, notably in satellite image classification where there is significant variation in lighting. We also investigate the relationship between Lipschitz consistency and weight decay, revealing that its impact scales with the spectrum of the neural network's weight matrix. To support our claims, we present experimental results using MNIST, Satellite Image Classification, and CIFAR-10, which show that enforcing Lipschitz consistency consistently improves the efficacy of small neural networks. To further explore the practical applications of Lipschitz consistency, we analyze its impact on a neural network's ability to provide reliable predictions for instances that lie far from the training data. Our findings indicate that models trained with Lipschitz consistency retain their accuracy even when faced with instances that are significantly different from the satellite images used for training. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/---/Lipschitz-Consistency. Moreover, we present a discussion on the relationship between Lipschitz consistency and other regularization techniques, highlighting its distinct aspects. Lastly, we propose a number of potential future research directions related to Lipschitz consistency. Our findings have been published in the journal Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS) under the name Neural Networks Regularized by Enforcing Lipschitz Continuity. Our work on Lipschitz consistency was funded by the Office of Naval Research, and we acknowledge the computational resources provided by the University of California, San Diego, through the Center for Computational Biology. Our findings have also been presented at the NIPS Meetings in Long Beach, California, and the International Conference on Machine Learning in Sydney, Australia. Our paper on Lipschitz consistency has been cited more than 100 times in various academic works, including but not limited to the journals Neural Information Processing Systems, Journal of Machine Learning Research, and the International Conference on Machine Learning. Our research on Lipschitz consistency has further inspired a number of potential applications and extensions in the field of machine learning, as outlined in the appendix section of our code on GitHub at https://github.com/---/Lipschitz-Consistency. Our work on Lipschitz consistency has also been recognized by the Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS) Awards

The metric dimension of a graph is a concept originally used to identify distinct locations within a metric space, typically associated with points in $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. This concept has been broadly adopted and adapted for various applications, including in graph theory, where it determines the number of nodes required to distinguish between distinct vertices in a graph. This study introduces an innovative framework consisting of two parameters, reducing the dimensionality of a graph to determine nodal recognition and dimensionality for node identification. We examine and compare these two measures, analyzing their relationship and exploiting their connection to achieve upper and lower bounds on the reduced metric dimension of a graph. Specifically, we derive an upper bound on the reduced metric dimension for an individual vertex, as well as a lower bound for the entire graph. Additionally, we establish equivalence between two specific cases: the reduced metric dimension of a complete graph is equal to its classical metric dimension, and the minimum number of nodes required to determine dimensionality in a graph is equal to the classical metric dimension of that graph. We also provide a lower bound on the reduced metric dimension of a graph with a specific feature, along with an associated upper bound, thereby establishing its connection to the minimum dominating set parameter. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the reduced metric dimension and other associated parameters, including the minimum dominating set, domination number, and vertex cover number. We conclude by examining the changes in reduced metric dimension under graph transformations and identifying key properties of this parameter in various special types of graphs. Lastly, we address some open problems and provide a potential framework for future research on this topic. This study was originally published in the journal Discrete Mathematics, volume 345.

We conducted a search for binary asteroids within Pan-STARRS1 images by applying a set of criteria to photometric, astrometric, and characteristic measures.  We evaluated 5491 candidates remaining after the application of criteria, which included assessing the consistency of stellar sequences, orbital patterns, and light patterns.  Our findings were cross-referenced with lists of named asteroids and established binary systems, as well as comprehensive records of asteroids, to yield 248 previously unknown binary asteroid candidates.  We determined the potential binaries among named and established asteroid populations, and calculated the estimated fraction of binary candidates in each group.  The results show that the estimated fraction of binaries among named asteroids appears lower, at approximately 5%, in comparison to established populations.  We also discovered 14 potential binaries among the named asteroids, including Hektorin, a system linked to the asteroid 624 Hektor.  Additionally, we found the binary candidates 37F, 128F, 162V, 162X, 162Y, 162Z, and 162AA among the larger asteroids, with sizes ranging from 1 to 2 kilometers in diameter.  The estimated fraction of binaries among the entire population of asteroids with diameters greater than 1 kilometer appears to be around 10%.  The most promising candidate among our findings is the binary 37F, linked to the asteroid 37 Figa, with a charactristic light curve and a large diameter of approximately 2 kilometers.  Further investigation is needed to confirm the binary nature of 37F, possibly through direct observation or mission consideration for the Asteroid Redirect Mission.  The extensive list of binary candidates remains subject to refinement as new information becomes available, and is likely influenced by various factors including orbital elements, light curve properties, and relation to small moons in the solar system. Recently developed methods for using network data to identify and assess peer influences can be quite comprehensive, yet they often yield informative results at the cost of precise estimations. Contrarily, this work focuses on a more efficient approach to analyzing peer effects in a linear regression model, where the impact of a network characteristic on an outcome variable is linear, and the effect of a particular individual within the network on that outcome is linear as well. Although it assumes a linear relationship between the network effect and the individual-level effect, it does not constrain the sign of that relationship. We leverage a non-parametric approach to assess the validity of the model and examine the properties of our estimation procedure through both simulated data and real-world peer influence networks. Specifically, we investigate college students' academic attitudes within a network defined by academic connections, and determine the extent to which the network predicts an individual's own behavior, as well as the behavior of specific peers within that network. Our findings show that the removal of a particular student from the network does not necessarily affect the outcome for all peers, as the degree of that impact varies significantly across different individuals. Furthermore, we find that the removal of a student with a particular characteristic (in this case, a higher level of academic ambition) results in a greater negative impact on peers with a similar level of ambition, a finding that we describe as 'peer amplification'. Consequently, our approach can be utilized to investigate peer amplification, or other similar phenomena, in a wide range of networks. We propose several potential directions for future research that build upon our method. We also discuss the distinction between our approach and other methods for analyzing peer influences, as well as other social network analysis tasks. Moreover, we provide a concise overview of our results, as well as our methodology, in the appendix section. Lastly, we conclude our paper by examining the conceptual implications of our findings on the underlying theory of social network dynamics, specifically the balance between conformity and individuality, and the resulting variety of behavior within a network. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the various knot types found in proteins and examines the possible folding paths for those knotted proteins. A novel, topology-focused analysis assembles the bending histories of a specific class of knotted proteins – those with surface knots – into a distinct topological framework. This framework allows for the identification of specific folding pathways that can untangle these knotted proteins. By comparing the natural state structures of a particular group of knotted proteins with a specific type of surface knot, researchers find that only a minority of these proteins have complex, triple-loop knots known as triple trefoil knots. In fact, the majority are found to have simpler knots like the Trefoil knot or Knot 3.5. The results also reveal distinct untangling pathway profiles for these proteins based on their knot type, indicating that different proteins with the same knot type may have distinct folding pathways. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring data conditioning by learning an unconditional generator that maps noise to real-world data despite the conditioning generator. A common approach to training conditional GANs relies on an additional discriminator to ensure the conditioning generator produces data indistinguishable from real data, which may not be necessary if the task primarily involves data conditioning. We argue that learning an unconditional generator is sufficient to condition data by training a single generator using an adversarial loss function with reverse mode. This technique, which we call inverse conditioning, has several benefits, including reducing model parameters and eliminating the need for a binary classification problem. Additionally, inverse conditioning allows for semi-supervised learning by utilizing fully labeled and partially labeled data simultaneously. Our experiments on three datasets demonstrate the efficacy of inverse conditioning in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings. In the unsupervised setting, inverse conditioning matches the performance of standard GANs, while in the semi-supervised setting, it outperforms the standard GANs. In both cases, inverse conditioning excels over the conditional GAN. Our findings also show that inverse conditioning generates high-quality samples during the unsupervised setting and reduces the gap between conditioned and unconditional samples in the semi-supervised setting. In both cases, this is reflected in the increase in the inception score. Our work offers several innovations, including the technique of inverse conditioning, a new unconditional generator pre-training method, and a dataset augmentation technique based on partial swapping. These innovations have the potential to be employed independently. Our code is available at https://github.com/AminAmini/PseudoSelling.

The precise origin of gamma-rays in nearby radio galaxies remains a mystery that has been hard to pinpoint due to poor resolution and limited energy sensitivity in historical observations. However, with the significantly improved sensitivity and resolution of the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and the Large Area Telescope on board the Swift Gamma-ray Telescope, we were able to identify two gas-rich radio galaxies, NGC 1068 and NGC 6266, which are associated with disk systems and display distinctive high-energy gamma-ray spectra. We applied a new model that takes into account electron interactions with magnetic fields and disk particles to explain the observed gamma-rays, and by doing so, we were able to determine the essential parameters of these systems, particularly the size of the disk and the strength of the magnetic field, which turned out to be surprisingly similar in these two galaxies. This is particularly significant because it allows us to link their powerful jet activity to a more familiar phenomenon - a giant accretion disk in local stellar mass galaxies. Moreover, this finding is in alignment with recent discoveries of massive disks in two other well-known galaxies, NGC 1275 and Circinus Galaxy S, and it highlights the pervasive role that these disks have in driving the jet activity in low-luminosity radio galaxies. Despite the limited current understanding and the need for further analysis, especially of these disks and their surrounding environments, we are confident that studying these galaxies can provide valuable insights into the various mechanisms that control the distribution of baryons in galaxies and the role of jet feedback in absorbing or star formation and supermassive black hole growth. Lastly, we propose a new approach that involves examining a broader population of local gamma-ray detectors for more such galaxies and for studying these galaxies in other wavebands. This could in turn lead to a broader classification of the various types of disk systems and their relationships with black hole masses and the surrounding environments. The proliferation of wearable devices for monitoring physical and mental health enables rich biometric data, which can be utilized for precision medicine. A notable issue arises when trying to train machine learning models using data from these wearables, as classification tasks often struggle with limited data. This paper introduces the FedHealth framework to address learning from wearable data in a federated transfer learning setting. It enables the secure and efficient sharing of data for training machine learning models on multiple entities, facilitating a seamless transition to new devices. The framework utilizes federated transfer learning to train models on different devices without exchanging actual data, thus addressing the issue of data heterogeneity and device changes. The proposed FedHealth framework leverages federated learning and transfer learning techniques to achieve outstanding performance, surpassing traditional approaches by 3.3% in average accuracy on the dataset used for testing. The framework has vast potential applications in healthcare, providing customizable and data-efficient solutions for various biometric signals and wearable devices. The code for FedHealth is now available online at https://github.com/liangxing-7/FedHealth. The proposed technique can be combined with other approaches to enhance existing models, leading to better performance and accelerations in various biomedical domains. The current implementation utilizes PyTorch for modeling and TensorFlow for secure federated learning, enabling easy modification and extension. The framework has been tested on biometric data from wearable devices, yet it can be applied to other domains with minimal modification, facilitating widespread adoption in healthcare, sports, and other biometric applications. A diverse range of optical patterns can be generated and their interactions examined using a unified framework, the $c$-number Wigner representation, applied to both linear and Kerr nonlinear systems in resonators and waveguides. This approach provides a clear and unified understanding of patterns in both classical and quantum contexts, as well as the linear and Kerr nonlinearity regimes, and reveals a fundamental level of similarity between them. Specifically, it shows that patterns in these systems can be described by a set of Hill's equations whose solutions exhibit the same level of structure as the universal set of solutions to the Toda lattice. This structure takes the form of integrals of motion that act on the solution space, and allows for a precise characterization of the systems' and patterns' physical properties. It also leads to the discovery of novel patterns that arise in the course of soliton collisions, as well as in systems with beam amplification, and demonstrates that defocusing linear systems share many features with the Kerr systems, offering a potential analogue for quantum systems. Furthermore, it reveals that waveguide arrays differ from resonator arrays in that they have an infinite sequence of integrals of motion, which explains the long-term soliton survival phenomenon observed in these systems. This discovery enables the precise characterization of soliton patterns in these systems, and offers a potential universal theory of soliton patterns in defocusing systems. It is also demonstrated that the combination of linear and Kerr nonlinearity sharing many features can result in over-shooting soliton collisions, as well as in beam amplification, and that this combination in waveguide arrays results in an infinite sequence of soliton collisions, enabling the long-term solition survival, and allowing for the characterization of its patterns. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. Dynamic processes, continually updated and evolving over time, pose a significant challenge for correct and efficient performance. As processes are subject to flux, their interpretation cannot be static, and learning cannot be deterministic. To handle this challenge, a new framework is introduced that enables the development of dynamic processes whose execution is informed by data streams and experience. Based on declarative representations, this framework allows processes to evolve by updating rules, and it provides multiple correct ways to achieve a desired outcome. The paper demonstrates that, under certain conditions, processes developed with the stream learning approach will eventually converge to a correct solution when exploring and learning from data streams. The novelty of this research is reflected in two key aspects: the introduction of a framework for dynamic processes and the discovery of convergence properties when learning from data streams. The paper's results are applicable to various domains, including autonomous navigation, agent coordination, and learning from feedback. The developed theory and algorithms are demonstrated through concrete examples and pseudocode, and they can be implemented using various process languages, including the ASP framework. The paper's research is further enhanced by a comparative analysis with related static learning methods. The paper concludes with a discussion on open issues, including the handling of uncertain processes and dynamic processes in multi-agent settings. The development of processes as learning from data streams and experience is shown to facilitate correct and efficient performance in complex domains, and it has the potential to be applied to a wide range of tasks. The paper's results can be extended in several ways, including the enhancement of stream learning algorithms and the development of processes for uncertain dynamic environments. The paper's research can be classified under the category of dynamic processes, learning from feedback, and stream learning, and it has been previously published in the proceedings of the 2020 International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between algebraic and geometric advanced compactifications of moduli spaces. We outline some major developments in the field, focusing on central results and techniques used by experts. Although we cover various developments, our goal is not to conduct an in-depth analysis of every aspect, but rather to demonstrate the interconnection between main themes and key research strategies. We explore the connections between specific algebraic and geometric constructions, as well as the implications of these constructions for Hodge theory and arithmetic applications. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for future research, identifying promising areas such as integral models of modular forms, compactifications of moduli spaces of algebraic cycles, and the intersection of arithmetic geometry and geometric compactifications. By combining contributions from prominent researchers, this note is intended for researchers already familiar with the subject matter who are looking for an overview of current developments and future research directions. The associated papers, part of the I.H.E.S. 50th anniversary celebration, are also discussed in this note. Due to the burgeoning need for emotional support, cross-lingual sentiment analysis on social media has become increasingly vital. This task involves categorizing posts written in languages other than the analyst's native tongue in terms of their emotional content, presenting a significant obstacle. To tackle this challenge, we developed a system that leverages multilingual knowledge and incorporates a dual classification framework. Initially, it employs a dual classification approach to determine the sentiment and target language of a given post. Then, based on this information, it classifies posts with known languages. Our evaluation used a newly assembled dataset consisting of 15 languages and showed that our approach outperforms existing methods. We also conducted a trial that incorporated multiple task types and found that our system efficiently manages task conflicts and prioritizes resource allocation effectively. Our code is available at GitHub.

The simplicial bundle construction, initially introduced by Bousfield and Kan, has been found to possess a natural group structure when defined using the total simplicial bundle and the simplicial quotient map. This discovery's underlying motivation stems from the need to extend the concept of a group acting on a space to a simplicial action. The action of a simplicial group G on a simplicial space X is defined by combining the action of each group component Gi on the corresponding space component Xi through the total simplicial space X. The study goes on to examine the properties of this simplicial action, demonstrating that it results in a simplicial set whose components are groups acting on the components of X. The connection to the classical concept of a group acting on a space is ensured by incorporating a degeneracy operator into the action, which causes the action to become natural in X. This paper delves into the source of low performance in VRD tasks due to a high rate of erroneous positive detections, citing it as a primary challenge. We contend that the issue arises because current models over rely on category relationships as a default, failing to adequately capture the precise connections between entities within individual images. To address this, we develop a novel category-independent spatial model to accurately identify relationships between distinct objects. The proposed method uses a distinct representation to capture the observed frequency of object relationships, contrasting it with the perceived frequency of category relationships. This is achieved through an inference technique that combines the proposed spatial model with a relationship frequency learning approach. We introduce a novel task to learn this frequency, alongside the standard VRD task. Our category-independent spatial model was implemented using a set of 12 classes, yielding a 23% relative improvement in AP compared to the baseline. The proposed method has been tested on 5 classes, demonstrating a 13% relative improvement in AP. The code is available at: https://github.com/lingyu-92/VRD-Challenge.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of quiescent galaxies in the state of formation with intense accretion, located in a galaxy cluster at a distance of 9.6 billion years from the present. This research focuses on galaxies with significant gas flowing towards their centers, yet they exhibit mature, spherical bulges rather than disk components. Consequently, these galaxies lack the typical distorted bulge we would expect and instead possess an abnormally developed core. This phenomenon holds particularly true for galaxies with higher rates of accretion and higher masses. We believe that these galaxies developed their bulges and became quiescent despite being tilted out of balance, which prevented them from collapsing into massive, star-forming bulges like we see in collapsed galaxies at the same era. This led us to investigate bulge formation through gravitational collapse or by forming around central mass concentrations. In the process, we found that galaxies with intense accretion and positive gas flows are more likely to become bulge-dominated even in quiescent stages. Further study revealed that, in such cases, bulge formation is linked to concentrated star creation rather than massive collapse. In the end, we found that, in these galaxies, we're not seeing massive, star-forming bulges even after a billion years, which gives us valuable information about how quiescent galaxies change over time. This knowledge is crucial in helping us better understand the development of galaxy bulges and their role in forming and changing galaxies. In the process, we discovered a large group of galaxies that are similar to these bulge-dominated, tilted galaxies but are formed around central mass concentrations, which are drawn to us. Recently published research indicates that strong solar flares may result in the generation of high-energy neutrons, electrons, and protons through the acceleration of particles, as observed during the significant event on November 7, 2004. Despite the arrival of Earth-based detectors, which can identify these particles once they penetrate the atmosphere, determining the initial characteristics of these particles remains challenging. A novel mathematical approach has been developed to analyze data from bone marrow detectors exposed to the solar flare and has yielded several key findings regarding the energy, composition, and arrival time of the neutrons and protons in the solar flare. Specifically, the research suggests that the flare was composed primarily of neutrons, with estimates indicating a ratio of 4:1 relative to the number of particles detected as protons, and that the energy of the particles was likely 2.5 GeV, with an estimated acceleration time of 40 seconds. The data analyzed originated from the SOLAR-10 experiment, which was part of the Neutron Monitor Database and resulted from the mathematical decomposition of the detector signals using the RAMONA simulation tool and nonlinear methods. The findings have been further validated using separate detectors located in Turkey and Tihany, Hungary. The research underlines the effectiveness of bone marrow detectors sensitive to zero-degree measurements and exposes the complexity of solar flares through which scientists can better understand the extremely energetic events occurring on the Sun. The analysis has been shared publicly and is available for further review and use by the scientific community. The data and measurements presented in this paper are authentic and have not been altered in any way. The rapid dissemination of false news is not only harmful to individual users, who suffer financial losses and psychological distress, but also poses a significant threat to society, with the potential to influence elections and trigger financial market volatility. False news has always existed, but the speed at which it spreads today is largely attributable to social media platforms that rely on user-based rating systems to rank and disseminate news articles. As a result, false news is often created and shared before legitimate news can respond and refute it, giving it a short-lived advantage before being debunked. This research focuses on detecting false news as it emerges, an inherently challenging task that demands simultaneous consideration of multiple news iterations and counter-reactions. To address this difficulty, we introduce a novel framework called MeFIND, which employs a false news indicator network that generates a score indicating the degree to which a news article is false, and a neural process engine that refines this score based on the contents of opposing articles submitted by users. Furthermore, we incorporate a dynamic hyperparameter update mechanism into the framework, which allows it to adapt to changing societal conditions, thereby enhancing its performance in an emerging false news context. To validate the effectiveness of MeFIND, we developed two datasets consisting of social media news content and associated truth labels, one for training and one for evaluation. Our experimental results show that MeFIND outperforms existing false news detection methods, especially in emerging false news scenarios. Finally, we demonstrate MeFIND's practical applications in a real-world false news dissemination scenario. The code is available at https://github.com/ghulam-eisam/Multimodal-Emergent-False-News-Identification.

Quantum interactions between valleys in silicon's crystal structure are regarded as precise interactions that quantum computers need to avoid. However, our findings indicate that these interactions can be precisely engineered to facilitate fast quantum communication between two parts of a silicon chip. By utilizing a atomic-scale building method, we created a precise 'valley interface' between two areas of a silicon chip, achieving a valley interaction 100 times stronger than typical interactions. This achievement enables execution of complex quantum operations such as BEC-BOS transitions, vallel interferometry, and quantum simulation of the Pauli-Hubbard model. Moreover, our technique allows for simultaneous execution of two types of quantum operations that typically cannot happen together, specifically the execution of a universal quantum gate set for spin and the execution of a universal gate set for valley quantum computation. This execution of these operations on a single chip allows for execution of multiple quantum tasks on a single chip, making it highly efficient. Additionally, our findings indicate that we can change the valley interaction's strength simply by moving a single phosphorus atom, a control that is unique to silicon's crystal structure. This control over valley interaction's strength also enables us to create a valley interface that can be connected to a quantum wire, making it possible for quantum information to travel through the valley interface. Complex systems consisting of multiple components, whose interactions shape the overall dynamics, pose significant challenges in identifying the underlying framework and understanding the inherent mechanics. This category of systems, found throughout nature and man-made objects, is characterized by intricate relationships between components, rendering traditional analysis methods less effective. In a breakthrough, Graph Neural Networks have successfully penetrated the veil of these complex interactions, enabling actionable insights into the underlying structure and dynamic behavior. This study delves into the fundamentals of Graph Neural Networks, framing them within the context of complex systems analysis. Specifically, we explore how these networks can simultaneously uncover a system's graph topology and model its behavioral dynamics, or convey the inherent mechanics from direct data analysis. Furthermore, we outline future research possibilities on the application of Graph Neural Networks to reveal the underlying principles of complex systems, citing examples from astronomical phenomena and biological organisms. A significant challenge in treating stroke lies in identifying appropriate therapies to promote brain recovery and prevent further damage. Advanced treatments such as transcranial magnetic stimulation and cell-based therapies have shown promise but their effectiveness varies greatly from one individual to another. One key factor influencing their success is the state of cerebral lesions, which scar tissue and damaged areas can cause. To determine whether these treatments are beneficial, it's essential to accurately assess the size and extent of these lesions. However, manually analyzing scans for individual subjects is difficult and time-consuming, and may not account for subjective interpreter bias. To address this issue, we developed an automated method using deep learning techniques to accurately measure cerebral lesions, reducing interpreter bias and increasing the efficiency of clinical trials. This approach combines a variational autoencoder with a progressive neural network to classify scans and assess lesion size, all while accounting for variations in image quality and different lesion types. Human tests have confirmed that this method correlates strongly with manual assessments, providing a reliable and unbiased tool for evaluating cerebral lesions in clinical trials of stroke recovery treatments. This research was conducted at the University of Ontario Institute Technology.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved high performance on numerous natural language processing tasks, outperforming traditional machine learning methods. However, the underlying mechanics of these models mean they rely on vast amounts of data for training, without a clear understanding of how they combine structured knowledge. This lack of insight creates significant challenges for their actual utility in real-world applications. To address this knowledge gap, our research develops a novel approach to integrate structured information from multiple sources into these models through a new module called Ability. This Ability module can draw from various knowledge representations, incorporating both rule-based and graph-based structures, and it seamlessly plugs into existing large language models via a simple procedure. To demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of our approach, we pair the Ability module with three different large language models, applying it to three distinct tasks: knowledge-rich language translation, category-based text classification, and detailed abstract summaries of scientific papers. The resulting performance surpasses existing methods and showcases a notable increase in knowledge retention and utilization. The code for Ability is available at https://github.com/THU-PLAB/Ability.

In recent years, multi-channel speech processing has gained significant attention, and techniques such as differential microphones have been widely used in various applications. However, when one or more microphones malfunction or experience signal degradation, the available signal can still be utilized to restore the clean speech. Introducing the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), a deep learning-based model designed to enhance single-channel speech based on a two-channel recording. The DPCRN model employs two paths: the recurrent part processes the short-term signal characteristics and the convolution part captures the signal patterns, then the two signals are combined using a weighted average. Experiments conducted on the Interspeech 2020 single-channel speech enhancement task using the SiWES database and a two-channel version showed the DPCRN model outperformed existing baselines. Furthermore, the model's effectiveness was demonstrated in various scenarios, including with one faulty microphone. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ASR-Group/DPCRN. The model has been successfully implemented in an application, such as Amazon Alexa. The DPCRN model's simplicity and the positive outcomes obtained make it a viable alternative for speech enhancement in various scenarios. The code has been submitted to International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing 2023.

We introduce a key model assumption that the cost of hedging an option delta is proportional to the square of the underlying asset's price. A novel solution to the resulting integral equation yields an explicit formula for the collateral requirement. We further derive an analytical expression for a specific measure of risk, which is a consequence of the collateral requirement formula. To validate this measure, we generate random samples of option prices and hedge deltas, which serve as inputs for the collateral requirement calculations. These simulations demonstrate that the proposed risk measure accurately estimates the expected collateral requirement. We also examine the impact of changing market conditions on the collateral requirement, as well as the risk it incurs, using our framework. Additionally, we observe that the risk incurred by the collateral scheme remains constant for a given option. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive analysis of these schemes was previously unfeasible. However, the introduction of blockchain technology, alongside associated privacy flaws, now allows us to investigate the internal workings of a prominent cryptocurrency-based pyramid scam called Forsage. Through a detailed examination of smart contract code, transaction observations, and statistical modeling, we clarified the scam's complex design, identified loopholes in the code, and determined that it operates as a hierarchical binary pyramid, favoring early investors at the expense of most participants. Furthermore, we estimated the total amount paid to participants and found it to be approximately $285 million. The significant scale of Forsage distinguishes it from typical scams, which typically involve a single perpetrator and a small number of victims. The success of Forsage can be attributed to its automated and decentralized design, which reduces operating expenses and enhances anonymity. Yet, the scheme's fundamental nature remains unchanged, ensuring that the vast majority of participants end up losing money. The widespread appeal of Forsage also highlights various issues with its target audience, including a lack of financial literacy and susceptibility to deception. The scarcity of recovered funds from fallen-out scammers like Forsage adds another challenging problem that needs urgent attention. The comprehensive examination of Forsage provides a valuable lesson for the cryptocurrency industry, emphasizing the importance of closely regulating pyramid scams and the critical need for financial literacy among users of decentralized applications. Ultimately, Forsage's remarkable success serves as a prime example of an increasingly appealing investment deception method called the "anonymous hierarchical scam." The research paper concludes by outlining various ways that Forsage's operators exploited existing loopholes and weaknesses in the code, as well as predicting the scheme's inevitable downfall and the resulting financial losses for its participants. The paper also examines the clean-up process among Forsage participants, the movement of remaining funds on the blockchain, and the broader implications of these findings for the cryptocurrency industry and financial literacy in general. The analysis of Forsage is further expanded into an appendix, where we examine the scheme's impact on specific Ethereum addresses, the distribution of funds among its participants, and the various ways that Forsage's code ensures the payment of early investors. The paper's findings have been made publicly available on the Blockchain Research Data Exchange. The catalog of the Milky Way bulge's globular clusters compiled by Ornitelli et al. (2020) was investigated using photometric and kinematic data from the VVV survey.  Baseline observations for the suspected clusters, including a new entry, were gathered, and 12 of the 19 clusters were confirmed, with 7 others requiring further investigation.  The 7 clusters with uncertain status are notable for having rapidly rotating central populations or extreme retrograde motions.  The most doubtful candidates were examined in more detail, and 4 new possibilities were discovered, including 3 small open clusters and a horizontal-branch object located in the Sgr dSph.  The study's results highlight the significance of the VVV survey data in confirming the bulge membership of 2 clusters with rapid core rotations and in revealing 4 new entities found in the bulge region.  The occurrence of rapidly rotating clusters with extreme retrograde motions may be attributed to bulge formation scenarios that incorporate counter-rotating mergers or massive early galaxy aggregates.  The release of the VVV survey's full catalog has the potential to explore the detailed properties of these suspect clusters, and future studies on their stellar populations, star formation rates, and chemodynamic histories are likely to yield valuable insights. The findings mentioned in this paper were discussed at the bulge formation meeting in 2019 and the meeting on globular cluster formation in 2020. We investigate positive definite functions expressed as inversions of classical Fourier transforms and define a space, FTBD, consisting of functions with bounded decay in both the Fourier and time domains. This space can be viewed as the intersection of two areas, one with polynomial decay in the frequency domain and another with exponential decay in the time domain, indicating a connection between Fourier analysis and the Gelfand-Shilov spaces. Specifically, we demonstrate that the presence of continuously differentiable characters is necessary and sufficient for the nontriviality of the space FTBD, which in turn is equivalent to the existence of certain C^2 characters. As a result, we derive conditions under which the space C^2_char is nontrivial, providing a solution to a problem posed by H. Obloza and G. Ahanger in 1990. Moreover, this nontriviality condition also implies the continuity of Toeplitz operators with symbols in BMO, which in turn leads to the extension of results by H. Ogawa and his colleagues to a more general setting. Finally, we establish an approach to investigating the continuity of more general Toeplitz operators by examining the relationship between the space of continuous characters and the space of measures equivalent to invariant Dirac measures. In the context of complex systems evolving over time, clustering is a key technique to gain insights by identifying distinct groups with varying behaviors. Unlike static systems, where clustering is well-established, dynamic systems present additional challenges due to shifting data points over time. The problem of modeling dynamic systems using state, output, and external input as features has been studied, but the optimal set of variables is often unknown in advance. To address this issue, a method is proposed to automatically determine the influential variables for clustering based on historical data, with an evaluation using a simulated example and real-data from a rolling mill. The proposed approach demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional methods, with possible applications in industries and research involving dynamic systems. The code is available at https://github.com/NeuralDynamicalSystems/DataGuidedInfluenceBasedClustering.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) rely on two interconnected components: a generator creating fake data resembling the target distribution and a discriminator differentiating real data from fabricated information. In standard GAN training, both the generator and discriminator are equally developed through simultaneous training, which can result in the generator outperforming the discriminator by creating very realistic data with a high realiability score. This issue is particularly pronounced in sparse labeling scenarios, such as text creation, where both the generator and discriminator need to compete for limited labeled data. To address this challenge, our SparseGAN model proposes a novel GAN architecture where the generator and discriminator train separately, leveraging a separate dataset for generator development. This separate training enables the generator to develop a rich understanding of the target distribution. We evaluate SparseGAN on multiple datasets and task settings, including sparse text classification, where it consistently outperforms traditional GANs. Additionally, we demonstrate SparseGAN's versatility and applicability to general text generation tasks. The corresponding code is available at https://github.com/PranavTyagi/SparseGAN.

However, this approach requires modeling these factors rigorously in order to accurately estimate population parameters. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a higher level of accuracy than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the transmission of solutions within multilayer networks of oscillators by reducing them to a standardized form. This approach enables us to investigate the transmission of solutions by considering the connection between the oscillator in question and a representative layer, specifically without accounting for the diversity of layer structures. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach to a wide range of multilayer networks by incorporating directed connections, different connection patterns in each layer, and layered structures featuring connections between layers. Ultimately, our method provides a unified understanding of the transmission of solutions in multilayer networks, as well as a framework for exploring more complicated scenarios. The supplementary material available online expands on our results to include a comprehensive list of the oscillator systems studied, along with a discussion of the challenges posed by discrete-time networks, a model involving partial transmission, and a model involving multilayer networks with the property of global connectivity. We examine the challenge of developing accurate representations of large networks from limited local views in networks that are prone to malicious node attacks. To achieve a comprehensive map of the network at an aggregate level, we propose a distributed estimation approach called VSSLE. This method ensures that the proposed estimator is unbiased and has a variance that is directly dependent on the number of influential nodes within a small, local neighborhood. However, the presence of malicious nodes compromised with the system failure can significantly impact the accuracy of the estimator. We have conducted a range of simulations on random, synthetic networks with features of small-world characteristics and found that the variance of the VSSLE estimator varies greatly, initially slowly increasing with network size before it climbs more rapidly as the network becomes more compact. We have also investigated the impact of malicious nodes on network size and found that the variance remains relatively steady before escalating more rapidly as the network becomes more compact. Finally, we have explored approaches to improve the estimation by expanding the local neighborhood without fully connecting to the network and found that a specific approach that prioritizes node selection based on degree can significantly improve the accuracy of the estimator in networks with compact structures. We have validated our proposed algorithm through a realistic dataset consisting of a small world Facebook network and observed similar patterns of simulation results. Lastly, we have a range of discussions on possible improvements, potential issues with our current approach, and possible applications of our methodology. We have made the code for our proposed algorithm publicly available. The code is based on the C++ programming language and can be executed on Linux operating systems. The code consists of approximately 300 lines of C++ code. The network dataset used in our experiments is also publicly available. The code and dataset for our experiments can be accessed at the URL https://github.com/author-name/Network-Scale-Estimation-under-Byzantine-Failures.
