Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN layers, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We observe an unusual Hall coefficient and anomalous Nernst coefficient ratio in Mn$_3$NiN, distinct from other materials. Furthermore, our results classify Mn$_3$NiN as an exceptional material exhibiting both positive and negative anomalous Nernst effects depending on the temperature and layer thickness, respectively. Our study highlights the Mn$_3$NiN material model as a promising basis for scientific investigation and demonstrates the importance of exploring antiferromagnetic antiperovskites in the study of anomaly-driven thermal transportation. We propose layers of Mn$_3$NiN as a suitable platform to demonstrate the anomalous Nernst effect in an all-oxide structure, enabled by suitable oxide buffers. We also suggest potential applications for this material, including thermal to electric energy conversion and thermophotonic devices, and propose experiments to investigate exfoliated Mn$_3$NiN flakes and oxide buffer layers for this purpose.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for use in safety-critical applications such as aircraft construction. However, the risk of sudden and catastrophic failure due to sudden crack growth remains a concern. A genetic algorithm in conjunction with Electrical Impedance Tomography can be used to accurately identify cracks in these materials by determining the optimal electrode placement for maximum resolution. Once the location of cracks is determined, we can guarantee the position of new failures by optimizing the placement in relation to existing damage, thus ensuring that future failures occur outside of previously identified damage regions. This innovative method can be used for multiple types of composites, varying in degree of sensitivity, and has been proven to be highly effective in real-world scenarios. Overall, this technique provides a groundbreaking way to ensure the safety and reliability of composite materials in critical applications. Ultimately, we hope to contribute to a deeper understanding of how to effectively combine individual components into a harmonious whole, and provide a foundation for further research into the nature of complex systems and their representation.

Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in patients with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body recovery but have yet to achieve successful restoration of lower body mobility with the exception of a few reported cases. To address this limitation, our research focused on understanding the central mechanisms underlying walking through analysis of electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals recorded directly from the motor cortex during induced walking paradigms in paraplegia patients. Our primary findings reveal that specific ambulatory states, such as standing and walking, are associated with distinct cortical activity patterns. Furthermore, our research demonstrated that walking-related walking state variables, including step frequency, can be accurately predicted through machine learning interpretation of these ECoG signals. Our results demonstrate that this method allows for precise prediction of step frequency with a mean absolute error of approximately 3.05 steps per minute. To extend our findings to non-parable individuals, we tested the system and found that it could estimate step frequency with a mean absolute error of approximately 5 steps per minute. Our research provides a foundational understanding of the central mechanisms underlying walking and demonstrates a novel BCI system capable of recovering lower body mobility in paraplegic patients. Identifying changes in the connection structure between different time series variables over time is a complex task, given the need to detect relationships that may be both nonlinear and shifting, often in presence of sudden disturbances. While recent advancements have explored the application of graph neural networks to dynamic graph learning, these methods generally suffer from lack of robustness to large changes in connections, due to their tendency to be biased towards connecting similar variables. In response to these limitations, a new framework is introduced that utilizes graph neural networks to automatically discover the connection structure between time series variables, with options for time-dependent connections, and then employs a switching algorithm to efficiently capture dynamic changes, even in presence of abrupt distortions. The proposed approach is evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets, with the results showing significant improvements over current methods in detecting both gradual and abrupt changes. The introduced method has further been applied to the analysis of stock market portfolios, with the derived dynamic connectivity revealing valuable insights into sectoral connections within the CRSP dataset of stocks. The code for the proposed method is publicly available at https://github.com/shahrokh-soltani/DDEC.

Animals play a significant role in various ecological processes, requiring their geographical tracks to be identified and analyzed. While camera traps provide a vast amount of footage containing wildlife videos, manually scanning through them to locate relevant videos is a substantial challenge. This issue can be resolved with the assistance of artificial intelligence, as we have developed a method to automatically filter out videos featuring biological movement. This approach involves combining extraction, classification, and selection techniques to accurately identify videos containing living creatures in a natural setting. We have tested and refined this computational approach using a substantial dataset of camera trap footage from the Kirindy Forest Reserve in western Madagascar. The results show that this method is effective in distinguishing between videos with and without biological movement, achieving an F1 score of 0.89 in the best scenario and 0.84 when considering all options. This research has significant implications for conserving biodiversity and managing protected areas through the analysis of camera trap footage, in addition to its potential applications in fields like zoology, ecology, and wildlife studies. The developed code is available online for public use.

Our research involves examining the underlying assumptions of QGP properties in heavy-ion collisions, specifically focusing on the initial conditions that are inferred from inclusive particle spectra. To achieve this, we investigated four different event generation models, including T\amp;C, T\amp;C with a Gaussian smear, DGLV, and Lenim, using frozen flow patterns obtained from our previous study. We compared the results to inclusive spectra measured by the ALICE experiment at the LHC. Our findings indicate that event generation models that incorporate elliptic flow naturally produce the correct level of elliptic anisotropy in particle distributions, while models without such anisotropy require additional constraints to accurately match the measured spectra. We also discovered that the freeze-out surface $\Sigma \Sigma$ obtained from the four models exhibits a $x$-$y$ elliptic anisotropy that aligns with experimental measurements, although variations exist particularly in the $x$-direction. Nonetheless, we found that the $x$-$y$ elliptic anisotropy is insufficient to explain the level of anisotropy observed in heavy-ion collisions. To better comprehend this shortcoming, we analyzed the initial condition distributions one by one, starting with the most influential $x$-direction anisotropy, and discovered that it can be attributed to the local eccentricity of individual participants rather than the overall anisotropy of the collision system. We achieved this modification by generating initial conditions based on the polar angle of participant particles, which successfully reproduced the measured level of anisotropy. This work investigates the extremal values of the generalization degrees of freedom (GDoF) benefit that accrues to optimal power control versus binary power control in interference networks with an increasing number of users. Specifically for a network with $K$ users, we establish that the extremal GDoF benefit ranges between the order of $10$ and the order of $\sqrt{K$10}$ in the context of an interference network with an arbitrary generalization parameter, and we further show that these two orders are asymptotically convergent as the number of users grows. Additionally, we demonstrate that both order bounds are achievable with a particular distribution of user interests in the context of a binary power control scheme, and that one of these order bounds is asymptotically attainable with optimal power control as the number of users grows. Finally, we propose a semi-analytical formula for the extremal GDoF benefit in the context of a binary power control scheme, and our simulations consistently indicate that this formula accurately captures the underlying performance characteristics. The research contributions of this work are rounded out by a discussion of its relevant connections to existing literature. The most notable of these connections is to an earlier result that held that the extremal GDoF benefit in a two-user interference network is equal to $10$, and our research further shows that this earlier result can be generalized to a much broader context that includes not just the two-user case but also the $K$-user case as well. We also investigate the extremal GDoF benefit in the context of a binary power control scheme with the added requirement that the average power level must remain within a predetermined limit, and our research demonstrates that this added requirement does not alter the basic structure of the optimal policy, and that the extremal GDoF benefit in this context is exactly the same as it is in the baseline binary power control case. Our research further shows that the added requirement of a fixed average power level does alter the underlying performance characteristics of the optimal policy, and that the extremal GDoF benefit in this context is directly proportional to the square root of the number of users, and our simulations consistently indicate that this proportional relationship holds true for the added challenge of user interest frequencies that vary widely. This research introduces an innovative integration approach for simulating multiple steps of a particle collision in fluid dynamics simulations. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, existing methods often break down into an inconsistent set of algebraic equations that are challenging to solve efficiently. Our new method involves a straightforward and efficient algorithm for addressing these equations, even for large time steps. We successfully demonstrated our integration approach for multiple steps of a collision in particle-fluid simulations. Specifically, we simulated the collision of individual particles with a flat wall and with each other, as well as the flow over a wall with particles colliding on its surface. This research focuses on advancing the design of a monopod for hopping on soft, uneven ground by conducting simulations and improving the initial design. The aim is to explore the feasibility of a monopod for hazardous terrains considered off-limits for traditional four-legged robots. The soft terrain was simulated and multiple scenarios tested in the lab to validate the simulations. A hybrid controller was utilized to manage hop height, landing position, and footstick, resulting in successful hopping on various soft surfaces with different densities and uneven ground. The effectiveness of the hybrid controller was demonstrated through multiple simulations and real-world experiments. The findings provide a foundation for utilizing hysteretic foam in design and offer a method for rapid simulation of hacking sounds. Furthermore, the development of a hysteretic foam model facilitated the discovery of a unique phenomenon called shear locking, not previously reported. The research was conducted by a single individual, although it's anticipated that future versions will involve a team. Our study examines the challenge of achieving high-temperature stability in correlated oxides with a d-orbital arrangement, akin to those found in nickelate materials, by introducing a dual-band model that accounts for both localized and itinerant d-electrons. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, causing turbulence and influencing the development of dust particles. Ultimately, VSI may impede the formation of particles by breaking down existing dust, but it also relies on particles to function properly. A balance is achieved when particles are somewhat large, allowing VSI to persist while continuing to contribute to particle growth. However, when the particles become too large, they hinder VSI, which in turn accelerates particle growth. It's also observed that VSI grows stronger near the inner regions of the disks, where it can cause significant turbulence. VSI's influence on the formation of particles is also examined in different disk environments, revealing that it may be diminished under sub-illuminated conditions, whereas its impact on particle growth is enhanced in regions with more accumulated matter. A balance is reached when the amount of matter and the level of illumination are both medium-sized, allowing VSI to persist while continuing to contribute to particle growth. It's also found that VSI plays a key role in shaping the layout and distribution of particles, contributing to vertical mixing and influencing the formation of gaps and hills in the disks. Ultimately, examining the interplay between VSI, the growth of particles, and their surrounding environment provides a clearer understanding of the complex dynamics within protoplanetary disks. A similar analysis of the instability that forms perpendicular to the sun, known as rayleigh-Benard instability, is also examined, which forms in the lower regions of the disks and contributes to the growth of particles, but has a more limited impact compared to VSI. Ultimately, examining both instabilities in tandem provides a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics and particle growth within protoplanetary disks. Recently introduced dynamic entrance networks have been shown to be effective in addressing sample size imbalance, by allocating different amounts of weight to individual data points during training. However, implementing these networks globally across machine learning systems has been challenging due to computation and memory requirements. In this work, a novel dynamic entrance framework called Global Mean Pooling Based Dynamic Entrance (GMDSE) is proposed, which simplifies the architecture by leveraging global mean pooling layers for similar purposes, while maintaining computational efficiency. Furthermore, GMDSE is shown to address issues related to over-reliance on dominant samples, and can be applied to a wide range of systems without significant modifications. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of GMDSE in handling sample size imbalance and improving the robustness of models with global average pooling layers. The proposed framework can be combined with other anti-oversmoothing techniques to further improve performance, and demonstrates its utility in various machine learning applications. The code for GMDSE is publicly available at https://github.com/zwang160.

This paper examines the impact of a unknown solar system parameter on parallax estimates made by Gaia-like telescopes, with a focus on a specific aspect that could affect the measurements of closer stars. This further reinforces the reliability of parallax estimates as a technique for measuring the distance to the stars. To effectively address open-domain commonsense question answering, it's essential to explore methods that analyze the connection between questions and available web documents. Current approaches primarily focus on incorporating rich representations, without sufficient attention to the semantic connections between questions and relevant documents. To enhance the performance of current models, we introduce a novel strategy, evaluating questions on their ability to generate high-quality summaries of existing documents. This approach enables the development of a compressor network that produces high-quality documents to answer questions. We incorporate this compressor's output in a comparative experiment with baseline methods, using the Commonsense Testing Dataset. Our results show that this approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both few-shot and open-shot scenarios. Furthermore, we analyze the underlying reasons for its performance, discovering that over 70% of questions are accurately answered by generating relevant documents due to their analysis of the question's own semantic structure. This research demonstrates that, with simple methods, it's possible to enhance the performance of current open-domain commonsense question answering models, and sheds light on the crucial aspect of semantic connection between questions and available web documents. We publicly share the code and compressor network at https://github.com/ghruan/C2P.

A systematic review is conducted to investigate the presence of knowledge gaps in previously studied spectral properties of molecular cations containing oxygen. Specifically, theoretical spectra for 37 cometary molecules, comprising 13 with single oxygen atoms and 24 with double oxygen bonds, were artificially calculated to determine their spectral patterns in the 0.1-12.0 micrometer range. These results are then compared to actual comet spectrum data from the Rosetta mission's OSIRIS instrument and two spacecraft: Philae's JOUVENET and MIRO, finding that while there are gaps in available data, particularly within the 0.1-2.0 micrometer range, these deficiencies can be addressed through experimental analysis of these molecules using techniques such as spectroscopic experimentation or astronomical observations from various spacecraft. Understanding and filling in these knowledge gaps is crucial for improving the interpretation of extraterrestrial data and for enhancing the ability to identify certain molecular cations in comet spectra. This paper introduces the random stroll method in Federated Learning, allowing multiple parties to contribute to a shared model using disparate data sets. Unlike existing approaches, we propose an efficient two-phase algorithm, where diverse data sets facilitate effective model enhancement in the initial phase and optimal optimization occurs in the subsequent phase. We prove that the random stroll approach converges to the optimal solution at a rate of $O(1)t\leq O(\max\{ \sqrt{K_L}\,,\,\sqrt{K_W}\}\sqrt{D_W})$ in the non-concave case and $\frac{2}{\epsilon}$ in the concave case, where the dimensions of the model parameters and data sets are denoted by $d$, $D_W$ and $D_L$ respectively. In the collaborative setting, we demonstrate rates of $O(\sqrt{d_t\cdot D_W})$ and $\frac{2}{\epsilon}$ for non-concave and concave cases respectively. In the experiment, we show that the random stroll method outperforms the baseline approach when the data sets are diverse. We also examine the efficacy of different stroll parameters, demonstrating the efficacy of the algorithm for complex models on large data sets. Furthermore, we present an enhanced version of the random stroll method and show that it yields optimal rates of $O(\sqrt{d_t\cdot (D_W + D_L)})$ and $\frac{2}{\epsilon}$ for non-concave and concave cases respectively. The results are validated through the simulation studies. The paper concludes by outlining potential future works, including the examination of the random stroll method in real-world applications, the investigation of diffusion methods as alternatives to stroll, and the analysis of the algorithm when the data sets change over time. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health issues, substance abuse, and poor physical health. The link between mental wellness and recidivism rates has been widely debated among scholars. Some evidence suggests that mental wellness can lower an offender's likelihood of reoffending, while other research finds no connection. To address this problem, a quasi-experimental study utilizing propensity score matching was conducted to examine the relationship between required mental health treatment and recidivism rates among offenders sentenced to probation. The analysis accounted for various factors that could influence an offender's behavior, both directly and indirectly, and compared two groups - those who were mandated to receive mental health treatment and those who were not. The study found that offenders required to receive treatment had a higher rate of reoffending and lower mental wellness scores than their counterparts not ordered to receive treatment. The results also indicated that the negative effects of required treatment on recidivism and mental wellness were more pronounced for offenders with higher levels of mental wellness. The findings have implications for policy makers, judges, and corrections officials, and suggest that assessing the impact of mandated mental health treatment on offenders who do not receive treatment could be an effective approach to improving outcomes. The study also highlights the importance of identifying offenders who would benefit from such orders and providing support for their mental wellness. The usual limitations of the study, as well as potential explanations for the results, including selection bias, reverse causality, and poor treatment delivery, are discussed in the paper. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing a new technique to enhance semi-supervised image segmentation. The proposed method involves training a network with two outputs: one for segmentation and one for classification, using only summary features from the encoder. By comparing our technique to leading baselines using publicly available datasets for brain and pancreas segmentation, we saw moderate to significant improvements in performance. Specifically, our technique showed notable gains with only 2D brain scans, demonstrating how our method can be effective in more constrained annotation scenarios. Our technique is particularly useful when working with limited annotated data and is suitable for a range of segmentation tasks. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub.

Quantum systems' behavior can be highly unpredictable due to their sensitive response to initial conditions, as seen in chaotic dynamics. Despite the importance of identifying chaos in quantum systems for reliable operations, assessing their stability remains a complex task. By utilizing time-evolved wave functions, our graph neural network-based approach determines the uncertainty of a quantum state's development. This leads to a novel metric that gauges quantum systems' chaos levels. To illustrate this framework's effectiveness, we apply it to multiple examples, including a highly unstable analog of the Heisenberg model, a randomized Hamiltonian, and the time-evolution of a chaotic scattering process. Our findings show that our metric accurately predicts systems' chaotic behavior both in a graphical representation and through comparison with a surrogate model. By further analyzing a fundamental yet chaotic scenario, we demonstrate that our approach reveals the source of the system's chaos. Additionally, we show that our framework's explainable nature allows for easy identification of erratic behavior's causes, even in more complex situations like time-evolving many-body systems. Our research enables a simple, reliable way to assess the stability of quantum systems with a good understanding of their dynamics. Our code is available at https://github.com/QTQGroup/ChaosGNP.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, fully automated theorem-proving technologies were gaining momentum, and various challenges and opportunities in translating proof objects into a standardized format were identified. Since then, despite contributions and advancements in SMT solving and proof checking, a unified structure for proof objects has yet to be established, and different solvers continue to employ distinct proof representations. This development is partly because a perfect solution has yet to be discovered, and partly because the focus of researchers has shifted towards developing solvers that can automate proofs entirely, rather than concentrating on the underlying proof structures and validating the effectiveness of their theorem-proving capabilities. This trend is reflected in the declining interest in proof-related challenges and issues, as evident from the diminished participation in recent PxTP workshops. In response to these developments, the Alethe system is being introduced, which enables solvers to express proofs in a unified and extensible way, and provides a vast library of pre-written proof constructors that can be tailored to suit the needs of various theorem-proving applications. The design of Alethe emphasizes flexibility and solver-agnosticism by representing proofs as a form of labeled ordered trees, and offers a command-line tool for validating the correctness of proof objects and checking their compatibility with certain theorem-proving standards. Furthermore, Alethe includes a module for converting proofs into a human-readable format, which can be utilized for demonstrating the capabilities of the system and educating students about the process of writing proofs. The capabilities of Alethe have been demonstrated through successful implementations in various applications, such as developing educational tools and validating the validity of random formula-generated proofs. The design and functionality of Alethe are available to the public under an permissive license, and the system can be used by solvers and educators who are interested in proving, educating, or developing solvers. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing their updates can become a major obstacle. The asymptotic optimization performance of leading algorithms under unconstrained gradient updates is not well-characterized in benchmark experiments. To address this gap, we conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the performance of buffered asynchronous accumulation in conjunction with unconstrained gradient updates. Our findings serve as a baseline to be surpassed to guide the development of optimized algorithms. We also explore a new version of buffered asynchronous accumulation, asymptotically matching the optimization performance of leading algorithms while providing a simpler and more scalable implementation. This version can be directly applied to various task domains. We further provide a theoretical performance analysis of the new version of buffered asynchronous accumulation. Our results demonstrate that in contrast to fixed learning rates, its convergence rate is insensitive to the scale of the unconstrained gradient updates. To further validate the efficacy of buffered asynchronous accumulation, we conduct real-world experiments on unconstrained gradient updates in cross-device federated learning. Research in navigation systems for marine robots focuses on combining sensor data with external information to adapt to dynamic environments. The connection between the robot's sensors and the external information can change over time, a phenomenon known as temporal variation. External information often comes from satellite signals, which can be affected by weather conditions, blockages, or signal jamming, causing the connection to become unstable and affecting the performance of navigation systems. In this paper, a new approach is introduced that uses a Gaussian Process to model the connection between the robot's sensors and the external information as time progresses, while also estimating the altitude of the robot. By representing the connection as sparse and incorporating prior knowledge, the approach reduces computational burden and increases the navigation system's performance in changing conditions. A comparison with alternative methods shows that the proposed approach outperforms them in scenarios with significant temporal variation. The proposed system has been tested on a marine robot in real-world scenarios with artificial obstacles and natural interference, demonstrating its effectiveness in navigating through complex environments with temporal variations. The code for this research is available online at https://github.com/Drone-Swarm-Lab/SPGTVL. The proposed approach can be applied to navigation systems in varying environments, not limited to marine robots. The proposed approach can also be used in other applications that involve time-dependent relationships between observed and unobserved variables. The approach has been successfully implemented on a marine robot navigating through a harbor with significant temporal variations, as shown in the video link https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V9m5VtL953A. The proposed approach can be further improved by incorporating more advanced methods to model time-dependent relationships, such as graph neural networks, and by developing a real-time implementation of the approach. The proposed approach has been tested in a harbor with a mix of open and blocked spaces, as shown in the video link https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V9m5VtL953A. The proposed approach can be used in various harbor scenarios, such as fishing harbors, ship-building harbors, recreational harbors, and military harbors. Most current sequence-to-sequence based grammatical error rectification models rely on vast amounts of data for high-quality results. However, correcting grammatical errors in languages like Arabic, Hebrew and Persian requires significant resources and poses a significant data collection hurdle. In response to this challenge, this paper introduces a novel domain adaptation technique that enables a model trained on one domain to accurately predict corrections on another, significantly different, domain with only a few example sentences. The proposed method achieves this through a feature extractor that spites the underlying syntax of the source and target domains, allowing for precise correction predictions. Experimentation across six diverse languages, including Arabic, Hebrew and Persian, demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, consistently outperforming baseline models by a 0.5 F score. Moreover, our approach shows versatility in being applicable to other few-shot domain adaptation tasks involving rich and diverse data. The proposed method's efficiency in utilizing sparse data efficiently also enables seamless integration into interactive tools like IDEs for real-time correction validation. The problem of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions may be mysterious, is a long-studied issue in economics. For a wide range of goods and valuation systems, a fair and efficient allocation can be achieved through a mechanism known as the Proportional Allocation Mechanism (PAM). However, the behavior of PAM is not well understood when the values of agents vary significantly. In this research, we investigate the equilibria of PAM in an environment where the values of agents are disparate and unknown, and where agents make rational decisions in a purely Nash way. Our primary findings can be summarized as follows: we first establish that PAM results in a unique pure Nash equilibrium that is both fair and efficient when the values of agents are sufficiently similar. Secondly, we show that PAM might give rise to a wide range of pure Nash equilibria that are diverse in terms of their balance and fairness, though not necessarily equitable, when the values of agents are disproportionately different. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these broad classes of environments are insensitive to how disparate the values of agents can be. Moreover, we establish that PAM remains robust and responsible in an environment marked by manipulative agents, tangible values, and uncertain values. Our research builds upon prior works such as [CR20], [CR21], and [CDW20]. We also provide a new characterization of the pure Nash equilibria in an environment with uncertain values, as well as a mechanism similar to PAM that can be used in an environment with self-interested and manipulative agents, tangible values, and discrete fairness standards. Our main results were initially established through the use of a particular family of functions known as submodular functions, though our approach also enables us to generalize these results to other complex functions such as the $k$-simplex, and even to characterize and generate diverse pure Nash equilibria through the use of a particular structure known as the Birkhoff polytope, among other things. Our research offers several key advantages over prior works such as [CR20], [CR21], and [CDW20], and provides results that are more expansive, more precise, and more diverse, in addition to the many other advantages it offers. In addition, we provide a characterization of the pure Nash equilibria in an environment with uncertain values, as well as a mechanism similar to PAM that can be used in an environment with self-interested and manipulative agents, tangible values, and discrete fairness standards.

The nova classification system was recently expanded to include superchands, a new category that lies between classical and recurrent novae.  We report on V392 Per, a nova that reached 100 times the energy of its typical pre-outburst radiation within gamma days of its maximum brightness, and for the first time is not just an optical detection of a nova by MAXI.  We determine its absolute magnitude at peak to be around -8.9, and that it took around 10 days for the nova to return to its pre-outburst level of radiation.  V392 Per showed significant nebular emission during its early stages, a feature that is rare in novae.  We confirm that the gamma-ray energy was radiated by the nova itself rather than another source, and that the nova was radiating across the entire electromagnetic spectrum at its peak, with a radiated energy equivalent to around 3 solar masses.  We determine the mass of the white dwarf in V392 Per to be around 0.8-1 solar masses, and that the nova had a prograde spin period of around 0.056 days, a value that is consistent with previous observations.  We also found that the gamma-ray spectrum could be explained by a combination of electron-positron pairs, and that the nova had a significant amount of accreted mass, around 10^(-8) solar masses, which is a value that is consistent with previous X-ray observations.  We confirm that V392 Per is a superchand nova rather than a classical nova, which is a classification that is supported by its low peak luminosity and the presence of nebular emission during its early stages.  We estimate that the accretion rate in V392 Per is around 10^(-10) solar masses per year, which is a value that is consistent with other superchand novae.  We confirm that V392 Per showed significant radio emission during its early stages, a feature that is rare in novae, and that the radio and gamma-ray energy spectra could be explained by the same population of electrons.  We estimate that the angular size of the radio source in V392 Per during its early stages was around 30 degrees, which is a value that is consistent with the geometry of a giant eruption nova.  We confirm that V392 Per showed significant optical and X-ray pulsation signals during its early stages, a feature that is rare in novae, and that the pulsation signals could be explained by the rotation of the white dwarf

Using geometric information from the image of a black hole, we demonstrate that there is an essential limit to the rate at which mass can be accumulated through accretion, specifically that the accretion rate cannot exceed a maximum value that is determined by the angular momentum of the accreting material and the mass of the black hole. When considering a long-duration accretion stream, we show that this limit results in an upper boundary in the plot of accretion rate versus time, which takes on a distinctive U-shaped profile. This prediction can be tested using current and upcoming observations of black holes, and provides a new metric for assessing the accuracy of general relativity in these situations. Specifically, we propose a quantitative indicator, called the Bondi parameter, which is directly observable and can be determined from high-resolution images of a black hole during a long accretion stream, thereby offering a means to assess the performance of any alternative theory of gravity. We anticipate that the most powerful event horizon telescope configurations will be capable of pinning down any deviation from the predicted value with an accuracy of better than $10\%$ when observing streams that last for a few hours, and conclude that the bondi parameter provides a crucial piece of information about the stream that cannot be replicated with other observables. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between the bondi parameter and other observables, such as the flux, and highlight the unique insights that it offers about the accretion process, particularly with regard to stream stability and stream types. Our research reveals that, whereas most such systems fail to form black holes through mergers, instead forming intermediate-mass black holes that stay at the cluster's center, those that do result in mergers producing black holes likely do so within approximately 10 million years. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 13 actions per second, largely because of strict safety checks required to prevent exploitation of flawed test designs.
Our text-based game, TextWorldExpress, shatters this record by implementing a more efficient reference implementation that can process over one million actions per second, a staggering improvement achieving a 50 times boost in gameplay speed.
To put this significant acceleration into perspective, it equates to performing approximately two million steps on a standard text-based game within the two hours allocated for the hidden state in the text-based chat game challenge. 
TextWorldExpress is not merely a high-performance version of a single game but a general-purpose framework that can enhance a wide range of existing text-based games by making them extremely scalable, and our results show that this framework can successfully accelerate a diverse range of games by another 30 times in terms of gameplay speed. 
This extensive text-based game benchmark came into being by integrating approximately 180 individual text-based games, spanning across a wide range of categories, and its easy-to-modify nature allows developers to enhance existing games with just a few lines of code. 
TextWorldExpress is an open-source platform available under the permissive Apache-2 license, and we are sharing the results of our experiments on a wide range of games at the website textworldexpress.org. 
This development has significant implications for conducting comprehensive tests on a wide range of text-based games, providing a solution to issues related to the lengthy duration required to complete certain challenges. 
For instance, the hidden state in the text-based chat game challenge can be shortened from two hours to under ten minutes.

We investigate the landscape of a particular matrix optimization problem, focusing on matrices of rank r, within a Riemannian manifold framework. This problem involves minimizing the difference between two matrices, subject to a trace norm constraint on the difference, and can be efficiently solved using a gradient-based iterative descent method. However, the convergence rate of this method is influenced by the precise shape of the optimization landscape, which is the subject of our investigation. We define the neighborhood in which the solution path is geodesically convex, and demonstrate that this geodesically convex region extends to the r'th trace norm eigenellipse, with a major axis length of 2sqrt(2r) times the mean of its semi-eigenvalues. Moreover, we establish that outside this eigenellipse, the matrix optimization problem can be reformed as a sequence of convex optimization problems, each associated with one of the eigenvalues. Additionally, this analysis enables us to classify the matrix optimization problem as a particular case of a more general problem, for which we establish the existence of a unique minimum solution within the space defined by its r'th trace norm eigenellipse. Finally, this conclusion is validated through numerical experiments conducted using both synthetic and real-world data. The matrix optimization problem under consideration is relevant to various applications, including sparse matrix decomposition, low-rank regression, and robust matrix reconstruction, among others. The findings of this study can be applied to these and similar research contexts. The algorithm used to solve this problem is available online at https://github.com/ShuaiHuang1992/GeoDecomposition. The results presented in this paper were previously published in the conference paper titled "Global Landscape Analysis of Low-Rank Matrix Optimization" presented at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 2019. A key advancement in 2020 involved developing an efficient and precise method for creating a substructure within an n-vertexted, cubic bipartite graph, known as the "edge-tinting" technique. This process divides the graph's vertices into two largely separate groups based on the connections between adjacent vertices. A significant discovery following this breakthrough was the discovery of a pattern to generate all possible bipartite graphs using a specific two-vertex configuration. A recent paper has been found that presents a counterexample preventing the inclusion of all cubic bipartite graphs through this generating method. A graph with 28 vertices meets this condition, denoted as the "Rosenfeld 28-vertex counterexample." A notable observation from this finding is that the two-structure pattern is versatile and can be applied to a broader class of non-bipartite graphs, specifically the "biparite" graphs, also known as the "mixed hypercube" with a 28 vertex variation. A previous misunderstanding about this method led to the incorrect inclusion of a non-bipartite graph, known as the "Doyen graph," which actually belongs to the bipartite category. A direct approach was used to create the Rosenfeld 28-vertex counterexample by systematically assembling the graph from a collection of smaller substructures. A notable feature of this counterexample is that it can be varied to include the Doyen graph, the mixed hypercube, and the 28-vertex variation of the biparite graph. A current challenge remains to determine if this method can generate the more complex hypercube of 34 vertices. We investigated a range of coevolutionary genetic strategies in a symmetric Cournot model, focusing on the interplay between firms' production levels and their corresponding market shares. We found that the most successful approaches typically converged to the Nash equilibrium defined by its stability properties, specifically being locally stable and unattractive to lower-producing firms. In contrast, techniques that relied solely on the market share as fitness, without considering production level, did not yield the desired Nash equilibrium outcome. To demonstrate the widespread occurrence of the Nash equilibrium in coevolutionary settings, we presented a theoretical argument based on the stability properties of genotypes in a simulated environment. The resulting genetic framework exhibited robust performance, outperforming non-coevolutionary methods in random and structured environments. Furthermore, we explored the relationship between the Nash equilibrium and the coevolutionary dynamics by identifying the corresponding genotype, which allowed us to gain insights into the emergence of the Nash equilibrium through genetic means. The findings from our simulation studies were validated through theoretical analysis, providing a foundation for understanding the coevolutionary establishment of the Nash equilibrium in Cournot games. The proposed genetic framework has applications in various fields, including economics, biology, and complex adaptive systems, where interactions between agents or individuals yield a pattern of stability similar to the Cournot dynamics. The code for the simulations is publicly available online. The emergence of the Nash equilibrium in coevolutionary settings also raises further questions about the firm-specific traits that define the corresponding genotype, which could be investigated through future research by incorporating additional factors such as firm heterogeneity, adaptive dynamics, or changing environmental conditions. The approach presented in this work can be adapted to suit these research areas, providing a blueprint for investigating the coevolutionary establishment of the Nash equilibrium in complex adaptive systems. The simulation code is available at https://github.com/ghpascual/NashCoevolution. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have gained widespread acceptance for various computer vision tasks, achieving high accuracy and a fast processing speed. Despite being reliable in many situations, CNNs are susceptible to performance degradation due to physical errors caused by hardware failures, temperature fluctuations, and aging effects. Researchers have been exploring methods to make CNNs more resilient to these disturbances. While successful, existing work on CNN fault tolerance relies heavily on numerical evidence and require more assurance. This paper provides a mathematical proof that activation interval supervision leads to robust outcomes for CNNs in the presence of noise and errors. This conclusion is supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental results. Evaluations using CNNs trained for image classification reveal that this technique yields comparable accuracy to baseline methods while demonstrating a high level of resilience in noisily operated environments. This is particularly evident in situations where memory and power consumption need to be conserved. Multilingual models are highly effective for natural language processing tasks across multiple languages, and these models are based on neural network architectures that treat languages as independent modules. However, incorporating knowledge across languages can significantly boost the performance of such models. We propose a novel approach to create a shared semantic space for multiple languages by developing a method to align word representations that respect the structure of clusters within each language. We demonstrate that this approach leads to improved results for both monolingual and multilingual tasks when evaluated using multiple evaluation metrics. Specifically, our approach achieves superior performance in comparison to other baseline methods for both text classification and sentiment analysis tasks across four different languages. We also explore our approach's robustness when different cluster structures are employed and find that it yields consistent results. Our method's effectiveness is attributed to its ability to preserve the unique cluster structure of each language within the shared semantic space, thereby preventing the overlap of distinct concepts across languages. We believe that our approach can be integrated into multilingual model architectures to create a more advanced and sophisticated system that leverages knowledge across languages. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulamai/MSSC.

In December 2019, a violent explosion of protests occurred in Santiago, the capital of Chile, which had significant historical cultural and political implications. Our study aims to analyze and model this event using a framework that combines epidemiological and social interaction theories. We applied the Kielsbrock-Schneider protest epidemic model, originally designed to simulate the 1993 riots in Theodorshagen, to the complex and dynamic Chilean protest scenario. Although the original model lacks an accurate fit for the initial stage of the protests, it effectively replicated the protests' subsequent decline with only a small adjustment, by incorporating a minimum number of suspicious cases below which protests cannot die out. We also discovered that the introduction of a critical threshold for protest onset may be necessary for better results. Furthermore, we found that the introduction of external factors, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, could significantly impact the model's predictions. Our study provides a mathematical understanding of the protests' dynamics and suggests that the model could be applied to similar protest scenarios in other countries. We also emphasize the importance of considering the cultural and historical context of these events. The model's code is available online, and we encourage readers to explore it and the associated results. The model's limitations, especially its incompatibility with the observed protest peak, present opportunities for future research into more advanced mathematical simulations. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and VIO techniques provide a way to achieve this by learning from sensor data. Despite successful applications, VIO systems often struggle with temporal consistency and map representation. To overcome these challenges, we introduce EMA-VIO, a deep Visual-Inertial Navigation model that utilizes an external memory attention mechanism to dynamically balance between temporal and spatial awareness. This model ensures consistent tracking and map representation by incorporating adaptation weights derived from the current estimation and prediction tasks. Using the IMU measurements as inputs, the model first generates state predictions, and then updates the internal state based on the observation of the current image. In addition to the standard VIO loss functions, the performance is also evaluated using a map matching metric, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of EMA-VIO by comparing it to basic VIO and fusion-based methods in complex real-world scenarios. Our proposed approach, FedSI, takes into account varied levels of knowledge base accessibility, as well as different labeling experiences among the participating parties. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes model, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes model's parameters and the underlying excitation-inhibition structure, despite the challenge of estimating the underlying intensity process that arises during such Bayesian estimation. By applying a post-estimation procedure that involves a contrast function, we were able to determine the accuracy of our estimates and reconstruct the intensity process. Our method also allows for a comparison of different complexity models, which is necessary because Bayesian estimation yields a model that includes the original data, albeit with low coherence. We have further developed a metric to assess the accuracy of the estimated excitation-inhibition structure, which is crucial for understanding events' interactions. Our method has been applied to real data consisting of 10 separate sequences of events, each of a different length, and has been compared to a standard nonparametric Bayesian estimator, as well as to a model in which the intensity process is Markovian, which is a special case of the nonlinear Hawkes model. Our results show that our method accurately estimates the intensity process and the underlying structure, and that this is reflected in a better fit to the data, as compared to the other methods, across nearly all of the 10 individual sequences of events that were analyzed. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Amir-Abdelparesh/Bayesian-Hawkes-Model.

We have originally assumed that decoding with the rank metric decoding (RMD) method would yield superior results when compared to list decoding (LD). However, our findings indicate that list decoding can sometimes outperform rank metric decoding, specifically when the rank error has a symmetric structure, can be detected, and occurs in codes with a specific, binary symmetric channel. Our primary contribution involves investigating list decoding's capability to correct symmetric rank errors. We have analyzed various scenarios, and our research reveals that when the rank error's matrix has a specific, simple structure (i.e. it consists of identity matrices), list decoding can recover it by determining the correct identity matrix. Furthermore, when the rank error's matrix has a more complex structure (i.e. it consists of a set of orthonormal matrices), list decoding cannot always succeed in recovering it. Our findings also include a specialized analysis of GMD codes. Our work builds upon previous research by the authors as well as on the rank metric decoding and list decoding theories. We have originally published these findings in an earlier paper titled "Decoding of Rank Metric Errors with List Decoding" in 2020. Our current work offers a list decoding-based approach for correcting symmetric rank errors in GMD codes. This is particularly relevant for code-based cryptographic protocols that rely on codebooks protected by rank metric errors. Our research indicates that these protocols can be made more resilient in the presence of symmetric rank errors. Our results also demonstrate that list decoding can succeed in recovering identity matrices or the original codebook, which in turn allows for successful execution of the Oxley and Williams (2020) randomised encryption scheme. Our findings for list decoding and rank metric errors are also applicable to non-adaptive multi-party private information retrieval scenarios. This is the case when the parties' shares of the encoded message are generated using a generator matrix that consists of the basis matrices of a GMD code. Our research further reveals that the failure rate of list decoding in recovering the original codebook is directly proportional to the rank error metric. This is particularly relevant for code-based cryptographic protocols and provides a performance benchmark. Our results for list decoding and rank metric errors are also applicable to randomised encryption schemes and non-adaptive multi-party private information retrieval scenarios in the context of binary symmetric channels. Our research indicates that the success rate of list decoding in recovering the original codebook can be improved by increasing the codebook's size or using a related construction known as the extended GMD code. This is particularly relevant for code-based cryptographic protocols and provides a performance improvement.

To investigate the structure of dark matter halos within $10.16^3$ cubic $h^{-1}$ Mpc boxes simulated on supercomputers, we employed a deep learning approach to focus on the relationship between halo mass and two key components: density distribution and velocity field. Utilizing a transfer learning technique from a convolutional neural network trained on simulated density fields, we developed a model that predicted density distributions surrounding halos. A separate model, derived from a convolutional neural network trained on simulated velocity fields, was then used to investigate the relationship between velocity field and halo mass. Our analysis revealed that the predicted density and velocity profiles can distinguish between halos based on their mass and shape, but the velocity field model also uncovered a significant impact of velocity field structure on the halo mass function. Specifically, the model exposed a link between the velocity field's granularity and the mass of halos within a given range. Furthermore, we found that replacing the velocity field with a component derived from the overall acceleration field removes the influence of this effect. Consequently, we found that the halo mass function becomes smoother and more linear when powered by this new acceleration field component. This discovery suggests that the velocity field's intricate structure, often overlooked, plays a significant role in defining the halo mass function, particularly over the range of masses we studied. These findings have implications for using dark matter halos as containers and the accuracy of simulations relying on the complexity of velocity fields, especially as future simulations with higher resolution reveal the same pattern of miscalibration. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static scenarios, uses time-dependent equations to determine the evolution of rotating star configurations. We have implemented this method in a way that combines efficiently with a multi-resolution grid approach, enabling the simulation of collapsing rotating stars and mass-accreting black holes. Our formulation features a new semi-lagrangian scheme, a globally conserved angular momentum tracker, and a numerical solver for the Einstein field equations utilizing a multi-resolution grid. This approach outputs equilibrium configurations in the form of time-series data, which can be identified by analyzing the temporal stability of simulation results. We have validated our method by generating a vast dataset of rotating star configurations, covering a wide range of mass ratios, angular momentum values, and equation of state parameters. This dataset is now available for the scientific community to use in subsequent simulations. We have also successfully demonstrated a supranuclear rotating star collapsing into a rotating black hole, and a model for cyberspace-based neutrino observatories that could detect neural signals from rotating star simulations. This research was conducted as part of the Antarctic research project Code Name: Snow Gong. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments, having an effective mapping technique is crucial. In this research, we introduce HiTMap, a novel graph-based mapping framework featuring a unique hierarchical topology designed to accommodate unknown environments. HiTMap incorporates an initial coarse-scale map to guide the robot's exploration and streamline its navigation, while a more detailed map is constructed in the background to accurately represent the environment through multi-scale mapping. We have tested HiTMap on simulation models of office and museum settings and implemented it on a mobile robot for experiments in office and warehouse settings. Our results show that HiTMap outperforms state-of-the-art navigation algorithms in terms of success rate in limited sight scenarios and demonstrates robust performance in real-world settings. Utilizing the theory, our group previously successfully explained experimental findings for a single manganese adatom and manganese dimers on the niobium surface by positioning the dimers in two different orientations. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from $500$ to $700$ million years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, making it possible for this planet to have conditions suitable for liquid water and potentially hosting life. Similar examples of such systems are rare, and further study of TOI-712 will provide valuable insights into exoplanetary systems throughout the universe. Although follow-up observations with spectroscopes revealed that TOI-712 is a subgiant star, initial radial velocity measurements indicated that it was a giant star, highlighting the complexity of determining stellar properties from transitation data and remote astronomical observations. Furthermore, analyzing metallicity in the planet's atmosphere using the $TESS$ spectroscope did not yield reliable results, emphasizing the importance of using space-based telescopes to study exoplanetary systems. Despite these challenges, the TOI-712 system remains an outstanding example of a young exoplanetary system that has evolved rapidly, and further research is necessary to understand its development and that of similar systems. Ultimately, detecting exoplanetary systems like TOI-712 in the early stages of their existence will provide valuable information about the formation and evolution of juvenile mini-Neptunes. Moreover, identifying planets like TOI-712 d, which are capable of supporting life, will be crucial in achieving the goal of finding life beyond the Earth. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO$_{2}$ using a quantum-kernel hybrid DFT method.  To account for the effects of static and dynamic correlations, the study incorporated a combination of pure and screened DFT-based interactions.  Our research examined all possible magnetic configurations for both C and N defects and compared our results to available experimental and theoretical data.  Our findings suggested that carbon defects are non-magnetic, whereas nitrogen defects exhibit magnetic properties, aligning with existing theoretical and experimental outcomes.  Our study also analyzed the energy gaps of static and dynamic interactions for both C and N defects.  We discovered that both closed-shell and partially-filled states can result from N defects, and that the fixed-nuclei calculations significantly underestimated the energy gaps compared to the quasi-relativistic evaluations.  We found that both C and N defects can occur in the Ti or O sites of the TiO$_{2}$ lattice.  Our data indicated that the most stable arrangements are those with a Ti-N-Ti or O-C-O configuration.  We also examined the effect of lattice vibrations on these arrangements and found that the energy gaps of the static and dynamic interactions vary significantly, with the most stable arrangements being the Ti-N-Ti or O-C-O configurations, followed by the N-Ti-O or C-O-Ti arrangements, and then the O-N-Ti or Ti-C-O configurations.  We found that the energy gaps of the static and dynamic interactions also vary depending on the direction of the electron and magnetic moment.  Our research examined all possible orientations of the electron and magnetic moment and found that the energy gaps of the static and dynamic interactions can differ by up to $3eV$ due to the effects of lattice vibrations and the orientation of the electron and magnetic moment.  We discovered that the most stable arrangements are those with a $90^{\circ}$ angle between the electron and magnetic moment.  We found that the energy gaps of the static and dynamic interactions vary significantly depending on the method of calculation, with the fixed-nuclei calculations resulting in the N-Ti-O or Ti-C-O configurations being the most stable arrangements, and the quasi-relativistic evaluations resulting in the Ti-N-Ti or O-C-O configurations being the most stable arrangements.  Our research examined the effects of static and dynamic correlations on the arrangement of the electron and magnetic moment and found that the most stable arrangements are those with a $90^{\circ}$ angle between the electron and magnetic moment.

This generalization enabled them to prove a significant paradigmatic theorem. Our presentation explores the concept of upper richness and related Ramsey theory, as we investigate the Ramsey theory of infinite graph components. Specifically, we determine the upper richness of various infinite graph components and employ this analysis to identify the Ramsey parameters for those components. Additionally, we establish lower and upper bounds on the Ramsey number for infinite star-lattice graphs. In a particular scenario, we demonstrate that an infinite star-lattice graph with a specific chromatic number has a specific upper richness, thereby providing an upper limit on the Ramsey number. In a more general case, we establish a lower bound on the upper richness of a random infinite graph, thereby obtaining a higher ramsey number upper bound. In a different context, we determine the upper richness of an infinite graph that contains multiple components, each with a different scale. In a more complex scenario, we establish an upper limit on the Ramsey number for a specific type of infinite graph with multiple components. In a further generalization of these results, we investigate how the Ramsey number of an infinite graph changes when the graph changes, as well as the subgraphs which contribute to the change, so that we can fully characterize the behavior of the Ramsey number for an infinite graph. A group G has an algebraic diameter of n if its non-trivial elements can be arranged into n distinct subsets, each representing a subgroup of G, such that the intersection of all these subsets is the identity element alone. We examine the properties of groups with a finite algebraic diameter and explore their relationship to various mathematical concepts including group theory, combinatorial design, and finite geometry. We also investigate the scope of these groups to cover all finite groups, proving that the majority of finite groups possess an algebraic diameter of n if and only if n exceeds their diameter by 2. We provide explicit examples of finite groups with a specific algebraic diameter of n, and explore the connection to known results and scenarios. Additionally, we establish that this construction is equivalent to defining a distributional vector field on the stack, subject to integrability conditions. This involves utilizing the geometric framework to generate a presheaf that forms a sheaf on the site of Lie groupoids, resulting from the separation of proper subfunctors. This process also enables us to recover the original groupoid as a quotient of the stack by its proper invariant substacks. We establish one-step prediction equations for certain classes of linear random systems with independent and identically distributed innovations on the sphere under static conditions. These equations hold without restriction and enable the prediction of every spherical random field at a given point, based on the values of the field at adjacent points. These adjacent values can be observed directly. We derive our predictions using the properties of the underlying inner product, and demonstrate that these predictions minimize the mean squared error. This result implies that the efficiency of these predictions is optimal, as they correspond to the smallest possible mean squared error. We also explore and calculate these predictions for several specialized cases. Furthermore, we provide evidence that our recurrence formula for the mean squared error is convergent, and show that the asymptotic predictions for points distant from the observed points converge to the best linear unbiased estimate, which is calculated using the Krzanowski operator. These results extend previously established results for one-dimensional systems. The statistical implications of these findings for spherical random systems with independent and identically distributed innovations under dynamic conditions remain to be explored. The methods used in this study rely on the Beurling complex autoregressive representation of random systems on the sphere. The evidence that the efficiency of the predictions is optimal is based on the properties of the Krzanowski operator, and the calculation of the predictions for specific cases relies on the use of spherical polynomials. The previously mentioned results are also valid for the disk and the parallel line on the Riemannian surface, as well as for the hyperbolic space. The behavior of the recurrence coefficients for the mean squared error and the predictions for points distant from the observed points can be determined from the properties of the hyperbolic polynomial, and the evidence that the predictions are efficient and optimal can be found in the properties of the Krzanowski operator. The calculation of the predictions for specific cases relies on the use of the hyperbolic monomials. The results presented in this study have statistical applications for random systems with independent and identically distributed innovations under dynamic conditions, with specific examples including the estimation of the mean and the regression coefficients for the sphere, the hyperbolic space, and the disk and the parallel line on the Riemannian surface. The results can be generalized to random systems with non-identically distributed innovations, with specific examples including the estimation of the mean and the regression coefficients for the sphere, the hyperbolic space, and the disk and the parallel line on the Riemannian surface, as well as for the hyperbolic space with changing radius.

The ability of artificial neural networks to generalize effectively is significantly impacted by outliers present in the training data, and this issue becomes particularly challenging in cancer research where dataset cleanliness is not commonly ensured. In this study, we employ a 3D CNN called ResNet to analyze three-dimensional surface models of skin carcinomas and differentiate between four cancer types: malignant, genarative, precancerous, and normal skin. Our primary objective was to determine whether this network can successfully identify the type of cancer represented by a particular model based on the types represented by the training models, as well as to assess the network's sensitivity to outliers. To achieve this, we introduced random outliers to the IISc Skin Cancer Hierarchy Dataset, which consists of 2000 three-dimensional models divided into four categories. Our results show that the network's performance decreases significantly when introduced to large numbers of outliers, indicating that it has difficulty handling noisy data. To enhance the network's ability to handle outliers, we developed a method to remove redundant models, thereby simplifying the dataset and improving the results. Additionally, we demonstrated that data cleaning techniques such as removing models with low resolution can also significantly improve the outcomes. Our findings also indicate that this network is prone to confusion between certain cancer types, such as genarative and malignant carcinomas, as well as between normal skin and certain cancer types. Our analysis suggests that this issue may be related to the way the labels are defined in the dataset. Our proposed solution involves redefining the labels in the dataset, which leads to a more organized and hierarchical structure and improves the results significantly. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that traditional attention mechanisms, although enhancing performance, can slow down decoding processes by requiring continuous re-computation of attention weights. To address this challenge, we introduce a look-forward attention approach, where the attention model is predicted upfront and remains fixed throughout decoding. This approach accelerates decoding by eliminating re-computation of attention weights. To handle situations where the target words exceed the source sentence length, we develop a proprietary method using the predicted attention weights to guide word selection. We also explore incorporating the proposed look-forward attention in various neural machine translation architectures and monitor its performance in conjunction with other acceleration techniques. Experimental results show that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in various evaluation metrics, demonstrating the efficacy of look-forward attention in neural machine translation. Moreover, the open-source code of our proposed method is available for public use.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus segmentation algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus segmentation in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus primarily on image reconstruction, the proposed network places a superior point annotation value as the supervised task, resulting in a fully automatic segmentation system with improved accuracy. Experimentation reveals that this model excels particularly in scenarios where nuclei are fused with each other or with the background tissue. Moreover, the proposed network achieves a top three ranking in the VinDrNet challenge, an achievement that is all the more significant given that the challenge data sets are complex and difficult to analyze, with points of annotation that are inaccurately marked. The code for the proposed network is available for public use on GitHub at the url https://github.com/ghruan/PointAnnotateNet. For researchers who prefer using C++ instead of Python, the code for the proposed network is available at the url https://github.com/ghruan/PointAnnotateNet_CXX. The proposed PointAnnotateNet model has been successfully applied to a wide range of medical imaging tasks, including lung, colon, pancreas, brain, breast, prostate, kidney, skin, cervical cancer, among others. The model can be downloaded at the url https://github.com/ghruan/PointAnnotateNet_Cancer.
