Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue properties by analyzing the movement of tissues during elastic waves are introduced and propagated. Accurate detection of tissue abnormalities is challenged by the precision required in measuring minimal displacements. The performance of elastography is particularly hampered in the vicinity of hard objects, due to their limited spherical imaging capability, necessitating the integration of elastography with ultrasound systems that employ synthetic aperture techniques. This paper presents a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture technique to enhance the precision of elastography in the lateral direction. By leveraging the precise displacement estimation capabilities of synthetic aperture techniques and the wide beamforming capabilities of focused arrays, the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture method offers highly precise displacement estimation in the lateral direction. This is demonstrated in numerical simulations and validated through the elastographic imaging of hard objects in phantom data, showing the technique's effectiveness. This approach has the potential to enhance the precision of elastography in real-time applications. The technique's efficiency has also been assessed in terms of computation time and the precision of displacement estimation, resulting in this study of a novel kind, where the performance of the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture method is compared with the conventional synthetic aperture technique. This has implications for the development of real-time elastography systems that combine synthetic aperture and elastography technologies. The technique has been shown to enhance the precision of displacement estimation in the lateral direction, with a mean precision of 2.05 mm, which is reflected in the improved precision of elastography in the same area, showing the direct relationship between the precision of displacement estimation and the precision of elastography. The occurrence of side lobe activity hampered the performance of the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture method in some cases, resulting in the creation of artificial softening of the image, which has been shown to be rectifiable. This has been demonstrated in the paper, where the elimination of side lobe activity through the application of weighted beamsforming has been shown to enhance the performance of the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture method in such cases, resulting in the correct imaging of hard objects in elastography. The technique's efficacy has been tested in phantom data containing soft tissues and hard objects of varying sizes, which is reflective of real-world applications, showing the robustness of the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture method in such scenarios. Imaging technologies for human-computer interaction have advanced, enabling the creation of visual proof systems that can convey mathematical truths to others. While achieving a universal understanding of these proofs with strangers is difficult due to their subjectivity, there is potential in leveraging task-oriented environments as a basis for these systems. In this work, we present a new framework, Rational Pseudocode, which uses interactive command lines as a model to securely convey algorithms to others. We demonstrate how various established algorithms can be effectively expressed within this framework and show that it is possible to validate certain aspects of these implementations, including specific functions and security-related properties, by monitoring their interactions with others. Furthermore, we showcase a versatile tool, the Rational Pseudocode Translator, which can take existing Python algorithms and successfully convert them into valid demonstrations. In a spirit of full disclosure, we highlight limitations in the current version of the translator, including its inability to accurately detect security-related vulnerabilities or validate the algorithms' efficiency. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit multiple-learning tasks by preventing the loss of information
gained in one task and facilitating the transfer to others. However, when
tasks are mutually exclusive, negative interactions can occur, causing a
decisive task to be impaired by the presence of a misleading similar-looking
fooling task that leads to an incorrect decision. In this case, a modular
system can succeed where combined systems fail, completely overcoming the
destructive interference by separating distinct representation spaces for
each task. We take it a step further by analyzing this concept within a
general model-based multi-task reinforcement learning framework, showing that
modularity also prevents harmful side effects of temporary errors in one
task from affecting the learning of another, and of different levels of
task difficulty. We propose a straightforward modular-based approach, and
to validate our findings we used a range of experiments, from simple
two-task scenarios like navigating an maze with loops to complex systems
with multiple similar-looking tasks and varying levels of difficulty. The
results consistently show that our approach succeeds in overcoming the
destructive interference and side effects, even in the presence of partially
exchanging state spaces. The code for the experiments is available online.

This task is critical in various applications, including hyper-spectral imaging, electromagnetic induction imaging, and semiconductor manufacturing. In response to these limitations, a regularized conditional GAN is proposed for posterior data extraction in inverse problems. This model leverages the conditionally normalized latent space and introduces noise in both the encoder and decoder to create a robust and general-purpose algorithm for extracting specific features from incomplete data. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of this model, demonstrating its capability to successfully retrieve specific attributes from inverse problems and its ability to tolerate noise in the input data. Compared to existing methods, the proposed model delivers superior performance in various evaluation metrics. The proposed model's capability to handle complex relationships and rugged terrain in hyper-spectral remote sensing imaging is also demonstrated, highlighting its potential applications in this field. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through diluted convolution layers. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive approach with convolutional neural networks but faces scalability issues due to its massive computational requirements and lengthy sample generation process. Furthermore, WN's pitch-dependent behavior is difficult to control and its trained models are challenging to modify for different pitch levels. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a pitch-dependent diluted convolution layer in QPNet, allowing for the control of pitch levels during training and the reduction of WN's computational needs. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that QPNet generates higher-quality samples at lower computational costs compared to WN, while also granting the flexibility to change pitch levels during training. Moreover, this study establishes an open-source repository for pre-trained QPNet models, enabling users to style-generated voices from any audio sample. In addition to audio generation, this model is capable of audio manipulation, as proven by the evaluation of six different scenarios. QPNet's simplicity and readability are also demonstrated by the successful implementation of a working example using TensorFlow Extended (TFX). The proposed model's capabilities are vast, offering potential applications in various domains including but not limited to audio generation, speech and text-to-speech, music composition, and music generation from limited available data. The code for QPNet is available at https://github.com/Aya-Metalsize/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

Further complications arise from overlapping speech, background noise, and moving audio sources.  Our aim is to develop a method that accurately identifies the source of each audio stream without relying on the speaker's physical appearance or assuming a simple environment.  Our approach combines a deep neural network that generates a spatial spectrum from each audio stream with an optimization-based algorithm that determines the sound source locations.  We validate our method against a robust set of real-world recordings and compare it to several state-of-the-art approaches, demonstrating its superior performance in difficult sound localization conditions. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach by adapting it to a related problem, facial orientation estimation, and report the results on a public dataset. We further investigate the theoretical aspects of LDGN and demonstrate its connection to the neighborhood aggregation framework, in addition to deriving an explicit lower bound for the learning capacity of LDGN. We introduce a new paradigm, the "most basic scoto-seesaw framework", which applies universal principles to reconcile the incompatibility between a light dark matter sector and a stable vacuum in the Standard Model plus Dark Matter. This framework's fundamental components, including the Lagrangian terms and the dark sector's structure, are defined as the simplest possibilities. We examine the potential for this framework to explain recent dark matter detection anomalies and investigate the interplay between dark matter and the vacuum stability of the Higgs field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the simplest scoto-seesaw frameworks are capable of ensuring the Higgs field's vacuum stability and provide parameters for all minimal types of these frameworks. Additionally, we analyze the phenomena associated with these frameworks, including the suppression of dark matter's relic density, the enhanced chance of detecting dark matter particles, and the influence on the vacuum stability of the Standard Model Higgs field. We also explore the possibility of these frameworks being related to the underlying principles of the lepton-seesaw mechanism. Lastly, we outline extensions to the most basic scoto-seesaw frameworks that could related to the standard lepton-seesaw mechanism, involving the inclusion of lepton singlet fields, the addition of Majorana neutrino masses, and the incorporation of the "charged scoto-seesaw" mechanism.
